readmePreview: Bun Documentation   •   Discord   •   Issues   •   Roadmap Read the docs → What is Bun? Bun is an all-in-one toolkit for JavaScript and TypeScript apps.

overview.summary: Bun is an all-in-one JavaScript/TypeScript runtime, bundler, transpiler, test runner, and npm-compatible package manager built on WebKit's JavaScriptCore and shipped as a single native binary. The codebase at this commit is a ~200-crate Rust Cargo workspace (`src/`) linked against a large C++ JSC bindings layer (`src/jsc/bindings/`, 407 files), ~15 vendored native dependencies, and a TypeScript layer (`src/js/`) that is bundled at build time into the binary as built-in modules like `node:fs` and `bun:ffi`. Everything routes through one process entry (`src/runtime/bin_entry/mod.rs::main`) into a single subcommand dispatch table (`src/runtime/cli/mod.rs`) covering 34 command tags — `run`, `install`, `test`, `build`, `pm`, `x`, `publish`, `audit`, and more. What's distinctive is the obsessive cold-start engineering (`#[cold]` on every non-`bun run` subcommand body, symbol ordering, mimalloc wired into ICU/libuv/BoringSSL before anything allocates) and a review culture encoded as machine-checked policy: `clippy.toml` bans `std::fs`, `mordant.toml` ratchets Rust lints against a baseline, and `REVIEW.md` distills ~2,500 merged PRs into merge-blocking rules.

system_map.summary: One native executable with a Rust core, a C++ JSC binding layer, and a build-time-bundled TypeScript module layer. `src/runtime/bin_entry/mod.rs` is the C-ABI `main`; it initializes the crash handler, allocator, stdio, and stack limits, then hands off to `cli::Cli::start()` which decodes a `Tag` and dispatches to one of 34 subcommand bodies. Storage is not a database — it's the lockfile (`bun.lock` text / `bun.lockb` binary under `src/install/lockfile/`), the global package cache, and the standalone-executable graph appended to the binary itself. Builds go through `scripts/build.ts` → CMake/ninja + `cargo` per-crate rlibs; CI is a generated Buildkite pipeline (`.buildkite/ci.ts`) plus 25 GitHub Actions workflows. Deployment shape is a downloadable binary plus npm packages, Docker images (`dockerhub/`), and a VS Code extension (`packages/bun-vscode`).

claims.claim: Process entry is `extern "C" fn main(argc, argv)` in `src/runtime/bin_entry/mod.rs`, which captures argv first (because musl static builds never pass argv to `.init_array` hooks), then initializes the crash handler, points ICU/libuv/BoringSSL at mimalloc, ignores SIGPIPE/SIGXFSZ, calls `output::stdio::init()`, `StackCheck::configure_thread()`, and finally `cli::Cli::start()` before `Global::exit(0)`.

The allocator is selected at compile time: mimalloc is the `#[global_allocator]` normally, but under `bun_asan` the build swaps to `std::alloc::System` so the ASAN interceptor sees every allocation; the binary also strong-defines `__asan_default_options` and `__lsan_default_suppressions` from the binary crate (not an rlib) so the link actually picks them up.

CLI dispatch is a flat `match tag { … }` over `bun_options_types::command_tag::Tag`, with every arm out-lined into its own `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` fn so `Cli::start` compiles to a jump table and cold subcommand bodies (`install`, `create`, bundler, test runner) don't share `.text` pages with the `bun run` startup chain.

`Tag` enumerates 34 subcommands and each carries a single-byte `char()` code used in crash-report URLs, explicitly documented as needing to stay in sync with the external `oven-sh/bun.report` decoder.

The Rust side is a Cargo workspace of ~200 member crates declared in the root `Cargo.toml`, tiered so lower crates (`bun_core`, `bun_sys`, `bun_paths`) never depend on `bun_jsc` or `bun_runtime`; `bun_runtime` is the graph root and every crate's rlib is an input to the final link.

The JS engine boundary lives in two halves: Rust-side glue in `src/jsc/` (`VirtualMachine.rs` at 7,700 lines, `ModuleLoader.rs`, `event_loop.rs`) and 407 files of hand-written + generated C++ in `src/jsc/bindings/` (`BunObject.cpp`, `ZigGlobalObject`, `BunPlugin.h`, per-class `JS*` files).

Built-in JS modules are authored as TypeScript under `src/js/{node,bun,internal,thirdparty,builtins}` and bundled into the binary by `src/codegen/bundle-modules.ts`; they are not ES modules — only string-literal `require()` and `$`-prefixed intrinsics are allowed.

Code generation is build-integrated: `generate-classes.ts` turns `*.classes.ts` definitions into paired Rust + C++ bindings, alongside `generate-jssink.ts`, `generate-host-exports.ts`, `generate-js2native.ts`, `bundle-functions.ts` and `generate-node-errors.ts`.

The build orchestrator is `scripts/build.ts`: it configures and runs ninja, supports profiles (`debug`, `release`, `release-asan`, `release-assertions`, `debug-local`), and implements build-then-exec arg routing where the first unrecognized arg starts the exec-args for the produced binary.

External integrations are first-class runtime surface rather than libraries: Postgres/MySQL/SQLite (`src/sql/`), Valkey/Redis (`src/valkey/`), S3 with SigV4 signing (`src/s3_signing/`), and an npm registry client (`src/install/npm.rs`).

Persistence for the package manager is the lockfile subsystem under `src/install/lockfile/`, which supports both the text `bun.lock` and legacy binary `bun.lockb` formats plus migration from other package managers (`src/install/migration/`, `src/install/pnpm.rs`).

CI is a programmatically generated Buildkite pipeline: `.buildkite/ci.ts` (1,997 lines) emits build steps, baked machine-image steps, and sharded test steps whose parallelism is platform-dependent (20 shards on Linux, 8 on Windows, 2 on macOS) with per-platform timeouts.

Twenty-five GitHub Actions workflows handle the non-Buildkite lanes — formatting, lint, Rust lints, source lints, bun-types tsc checks, FreeBSD smoke, release, docs deploy, and a family of automated vendor-bump workflows (`update-cares.yml`, `update-zstd.yml`, `update-libarchive.yml`, …).

Sibling deliverables ship from `packages/`: the public `bun-types` TypeScript declarations (the only npm workspace in the root `package.json`), a VS Code extension, a debug-adapter/inspector protocol pair, a Lambda layer, and native plugin APIs for Rust and C.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface splits four ways: the CLI subcommand table, the `Bun` global namespace, the Node.js compatibility layer, and Web APIs. The CLI covers running scripts, package management (install/add/update/remove/link/patch/publish/audit/why/dedupe/prune/outdated), bundling (`bun build`, including `--compile` standalone executables), testing (`bun test`), a REPL, `bunx`, `bun init`/`bun create`, and self-upgrade. The `Bun` global is defined by a JSC hash table in `BunObject.cpp` exposing ~100 properties — `Bun.serve`, `Bun.file`, `Bun.write`, `Bun.spawn`, `Bun.build`, `Bun.sql`, `Bun.redis`, `Bun.s3`, `Bun.secrets`, `Bun.CSRF`, `Bun.$` shell, FFI, and hashing/compression helpers. Node compatibility is implemented per-module across `src/js/node/*.ts` and `src/runtime/node/*.rs`. Bake (`src/runtime/bake/`) adds a hot-reloading dev server and server-components framework toolkit on top of the bundler and `Bun.serve`.

claims.claim: The CLI exposes 34 dispatchable commands including `run`, `test`, `build`, `install`, `add`, `update`, `remove`, `link`/`unlink`, `patch`/`patch-commit`, `outdated`, `update --interactive`, `publish`, `audit`, `why`, `dedupe`, `prune`, `pm`, `x` (bunx), `repl`, `exec`, `init`, `create`, `upgrade`, and a `fuzzilli` fuzzing entry point.

`bun pm` is itself a subcommand hub with its own verbs — `pm ls`, `pm why`, `pm view`, `pm pkg`, `pm licenses`, `pm trust`/`untrusted`/`default-trusted`, `pm version`, and a `pm diff` implementation split across five files (`pm_diff_command.rs`, `pm_diff_semantic.rs`, `pm_diff_normalize.rs`, `pm_diff_relayout.rs`, `pm_diff_profile.rs`).

The `Bun` global's full property list is a JSC static hash table in `BunObject.cpp`, including `serve`, `file`, `write`, `spawn`/`spawnSync`, `build`, `listen`/`connect`/`udpSocket`, `password`, `hash`, `which`, `mmap`, `inspect`, `peek`, `plugin`, `Transpiler`, `embeddedFiles`, `randomUUIDv5`/`v7`, `stringWidth`/`stripANSI`/`wrapAnsi`, and `generateHeapSnapshot`.
Data-format parsers are exposed as lazily constructed `Bun` properties: `Bun.TOML`, `Bun.YAML`, `Bun.XML`, `Bun.JSON5`, `Bun.JSONC`, `Bun.JSONL`, and `Bun.markdown`, backed by dedicated Rust objects.

`Bun.serve()` is implemented as a const-generic `NewServer<SSL, DEBUG>` monomorphized four ways (HTTP/HTTPS × normal/debug) over uWebSockets, with per-request state in a 4,794-line `RequestContext.rs` that also handles WebSocket upgrades, range requests, and cookie maps.

Bake is a dev-server + SSR framework toolkit that attaches to `Bun.serve`, holds all build state in memory with an incremental graph, and is explicitly designed as infrastructure for frameworks rather than being a framework itself; it ships a React framework (`src/runtime/bake/bun-framework-react`) and an HMR client runtime.

`bun build --compile` produces standalone executables by appending a `bun_standalone_graph::Graph` to the binary; boot takes a dedicated `#[cold]` path that splices `compile_exec_argv` and `BUN_OPTIONS` into argv before handing off to `RunCommand::boot_standalone`.

The test runner is a Jest-compatible implementation in `src/runtime/test_runner/` with `expect` matchers, snapshot support, structured diffing, and a `CommandLineReporter` driven from `test_command.rs::run_all_tests`.

Node.js compatibility is implemented module-by-module in TypeScript (`src/js/node/` — `fs`, `http`, `http2`, `net`, `tls`, `dgram`, `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `vm`, `quic`, `wasi`, `inspector`, `domain`, `trace_events`) with native bindings alongside in `src/runtime/node/` (`node_fs.rs` is the second-largest Rust file in the repo).

Web/platform APIs live in `src/runtime/webcore/`: `fetch`, `Request`/`Response`, `Blob`, `FormData`, `ReadableStream` and sinks, `TextEncoder`/`TextDecoder`, `CompressionStream`, `CookieMap`, `FileReader`, `Crypto`, and an `ObjectURLRegistry`.

`bun:ffi` compiles C at runtime via a vendored TinyCC (`bun_tcc_sys::State`), exposing `cc`, `linkSymbols`, `dlopen`, and JS callbacks, with bundled stdlib headers shipped as source files next to the implementation.
`Bun.secrets` is an OS-keychain integration with three platform backends — macOS Keychain, Linux libsecret, and Windows Credential Manager — behind one JS object.

`Bun.$` shell is a full cross-platform shell implementation with its own parser (`src/shell_parser/`), brace expansion, an interpreter state machine, and built-in commands so scripts don't depend on a system shell.
There is an experimental `Bun.WebView` API with native backends — a WebKit backend, a Chrome backend driven over an IPC protocol, and a separate host process.

`bun install` supports two linker strategies selected by `NodeLinker` — classic hoisted installs (`hoisted_install.rs`) and pnpm-style isolated store installs (`isolated_install/`) — plus patching, catalogs, workspaces, and transitive update planning.

data_flow.summary: Three main pipelines dominate. (1) Source → runtime: the JSC module loader asks `Bun__transpile*` hooks in `jsc_hooks.rs`, which resolve through `bun_resolver`, parse with `bun_js_parser`, print with `bun_js_printer`, and hand a `ResolvedSource` back to JSC; results are cached in a `RuntimeTranspilerStore` and an arena that is reset between graphs. (2) Package manifests → lockfile → disk: `install_with_manager` loads the lockfile, resolves dependencies via the registry client and task queue, runs a security scan, extracts tarballs, links binaries, then runs lifecycle scripts and saves the lockfile. (3) Bundling: `BundleV2` owns a `Graph` of parse tasks fanned out to worker threads, then `LinkerContext` performs tree-shaking, chunking, and sourcemap emission. Cross-thread movement is explicit: `ConcurrentTask`/`DeferredTaskQueue` marshal work onto the JS thread, and the HTTP client runs on its own `HTTPThread`.

claims.claim: Module loading is split across the crate boundary on purpose: `ModuleLoader` and `FetchFlags` live in `bun_jsc`, while the actual `transpile_source_code`/`fetch_builtin_module` bodies and the `Bun__transpile*`/`Bun__resolve*` C++ entry points live in `bun_runtime::jsc_hooks` and are reached through link-time `extern "Rust"` declarations.

The transpiler arena is owned by `ModuleLoader::transpile_source_code_arena` and reset between module graphs via `ModuleLoader::reset_arena`, which takes `&mut VirtualMachine` rather than `&mut self` because `ModuleLoader` is a value field of the VM and taking both would alias.

Entry-point evaluation flows `vm.load_entry_point(entry)` → a JSC internal promise; a rejected promise is routed to `vm.uncaught_exception` with an `is_rejection` flag derived from `entry_point_result.evaluated_as_cjs`, so a CJS entry's top-level throw is reported as `uncaughtException` and an ESM entry's as `unhandledRejection`, matching Node.

Environment data enters through `bun_dotenv::Loader` wired onto the transpiler, is published to the HTTP client via `bun_http::async_http::load_env`, and on Windows the UTF-16 OS environment block is converted to WTF-8 in `main()` before anything reads `process.env`.

CLI configuration merges three inputs — argv (parsed by `Arguments::parse` into a `ContextData`), the `BUN_OPTIONS` env var (spliced into argv), and `bunfig.toml` parsed by `src/bunfig/bunfig.rs` — with `ctx.args`/`ctx.debug`/`ctx.runtime_options` as the state owner passed down to every command.

Registry credentials flow from two sources into one `api::NpmRegistry` value: `.npmrc`-style `_authToken` segments parsed in `src/install/npm.rs`, and `[install.scopes]` entries in bunfig where explicit `username`/`password`/`token` keys replace any credentials embedded in the URL as a set.

`install_with_manager` is the state machine for installs: prefetch DNS for the registry, load the lockfile from cwd, reconcile config version, diff the root package, enqueue dependency resolution, run tasks, then save the lockfile — with a `mark_loaded_packages()` checkpoint so packages appended by manifest fetches are distinguishable from lockfile pins.

The security scanner runs user-supplied scanning code out-of-process and talks to it over two dedicated file descriptors — fd 3 for the child's JSON result and fd 4 for the parent's package list, read to EOF — rather than stdin/stdout, so scanner console output can't corrupt the protocol.

Lifecycle scripts are spawned through `bun_spawn` from `src/install/lifecycle_script_runner.rs`, which is deliberately placed in the lower `bun_install` crate so `bun run` and package-install script execution share one implementation (`RunCommand::replace_package_manager_run` is a thin re-export).

Bundling state is owned by `BundleV2`, which holds a `Graph`, a `PathToSourceIndexMap`, `ParseTask`s, and an optional second `ssr_transpiler` used for the client half of a Server Components build; linking and chunking happen in the separate `LinkerContext`.

The dev server keeps every build artifact in memory behind an `IncrementalGraph` with the stated invariant that editing a file must rebundle exactly that file, and exposes a `memory_cost_detailed` breakdown so that in-memory retention is measurable.

Cross-thread data movement is centralized in `src/event_loop/`: `ConcurrentTask` and `DeferredTaskQueue` enqueue onto the JS thread, `AnyEventLoop` abstracts over the uWS loop on POSIX and libuv on Windows, and `MiniEventLoop`/`SpawnSyncEventLoop` serve non-JS contexts like the package manager.

Outbound HTTP is a separate subsystem with its own thread and protocol clients — `HTTPThread.rs`, `H2Client.rs` (HTTP/2 over lshpack), `H3Client.rs` (HTTP/3 over lsquic), plus decompression and certificate-info paths — and `fetch` opts into h2/h3 via process-global atomics set from CLI flags.

S3 requests are signed in the `bun_s3_signing` crate, which owns credentials, ACL, storage class, and multipart options as pure config with no JSC dependency, and the runtime's `S3Client`/`S3File` re-export it — keeping signing testable below the JS tier.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows walked end to end. Startup (`bun foo.ts`): C runtime → `main` → allocator/crash/stdio init → `Cli::start` → `Command::start` → fast-path detection of a run entrypoint → `init` → `RunCommand::exec_with_cfg` → `boot` → `VirtualMachine::init_with_module_graph` → `Run::start` → `load_entry_point` → event-loop drain → `on_before_exit`. Install: `Tag::InstallCommand` → `InstallCommand::exec` → `PackageManager::init` → `install_with_manager` → lockfile load → resolution → task run → scanner → installer → lifecycle scripts → `save_lockfile`. Serve/dev: `Bun.serve` constructs a monomorphized `NewServer`, uWS delivers a request into `RequestContext`, and under Bake the DevServer checks the Host header, resolves a route through `FrameworkRouter`, incrementally bundles, and pushes HMR events over a WebSocket.

claims.claim: Startup step 0 is argv capture (`bun_core::init_argv`) explicitly before `bun_crash_handler::init()`, because the crash handler's panic path prints the command line from `bun_core::argv()`.

On Linux, `main()` calls `pregrow_fd_table()` — a `dup_at_least(stdin, 1023)` followed by `close` — before any thread exists, because `expand_fdtable()` waits for an RCU grace period once the process is multi-threaded.

`Cli::start` sets the main-thread id for crash reporting, records the start time, initializes a process-lifetime `Log` and a `CLI_ARENA` mimalloc arena via `RacyCell` (sound because it runs single-threaded), then calls `Command::start(log)` and routes any error through `handle_root_error` after printing accumulated diagnostics.

`Command::start` short-circuits: if `argv[1]` `looks_like_run_entrypoint`, it jumps straight to `exec_auto_or_run(Tag::AutoCommand)` without decoding the subcommand keyword table at all, and only otherwise calls `which()` to classify.

`RunCommand::boot` calls `VirtualMachine::init_with_module_graph`, then moves preloads and passthrough argv onto the VM, leaks the entry path to `'static` (because `vm.main` is a backref and the runner never returns), wires the transpiler from the context, calls `configure_defines()`, and loads env into the HTTP client before constructing `Run` and calling `.start()`.

`Run::start` takes the JSC API lock and never drops it (the function is `-> !`), then in order: enables CPU/heap profilers, adds conditional globals (`Bun__ExposeNodeModuleGlobals` for `--eval`, `addGc` for `--expose-gc`), performs optional Redis and SQL preconnects under the lock, enables the hot/watch reloader, and only then loads the entry point.

After the entry graph evaluates, `Run::start` runs one opportunistic `release_weak_refs()` + `run_gc(false)` to drop transpiler garbage — but skips it for standalone executables, whose code blocks came from an embedded bytecode cache and would only need re-decoding.

The core run-loop has two shapes: under `--watch`/`--hot` it loops forever (`tick` → `auto_tick_active` → `on_before_exit` → `tick_possibly_forever`) so a rejected entry keeps the process alive; otherwise it drains until the loop is no longer alive, optionally prints the entry result for `--print`, and calls `on_before_exit` once.

For `--print` with a pending top-level promise, the runner attaches `Bun__onResolveEntryPointResult`/`Bun__onRejectEntryPointResult` (C-ABI shims emitted by `generate-host-exports.ts`), re-drains the loop, and then prints through `ConsoleObject::message_with_type_and_level`.
`bun install` begins by prefetching DNS for the default registry — but only when there is no HTTP proxy, the mode is not offline, and the registry hostname is not already an IP address.

Lockfile loading uses a single raw-pointer provenance root with an explicit SAFETY note, because `load_from_cwd` needs `manager`, `manager.lockfile`, and `manager.log` borrowed simultaneously and borrowck cannot express the disjointness.

The install path decides whether to force a lockfile rewrite by OR-ing four conditions — an explicit force flag, a changed config version, a migration from another package manager, and a binary lockfile encountered while `save-text-lockfile` is set.

Standalone-executable boot forces lazy argv init before reading `bun_options_argc()`, temporarily narrows `bun.argv` to executable + parsed options so user flags like `--version` are not intercepted by Bun's own parser, restores full argv, then computes the passthrough offset and calls `RunCommand::boot_standalone`.

The dev server gates every request on `is_allowed_host_header`, which accepts a missing-Host request never, then allows `localhost`, any `*.localhost` suffix, any bare IP literal (after stripping IPv6 brackets), or an exact case-insensitive match against the configured bind hostname — a DNS-rebinding guard on the local dev origin.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is dominated by 2,149 JS/TS test files run through Bun's own Jest-compatible runner, orchestrated by a Node.js script (`scripts/runner.node.ts`, 3,504 lines) that deliberately avoids Bun APIs and imports nothing, spawning each file in a separate process so crashes are attributable. Coverage is heaviest in `test/js` (1,307 files) and `test/regression` (426 issue-numbered files); `test/bundler` uses a dedicated `itBundled` harness, `test/bake` covers HMR, and `test/internal` tests the build scripts themselves. Rust has thin unit coverage — 76 files contain `#[test]` out of ~700 Rust source files. CI shards the suite 20 ways on Linux with ASAN options set, and non-binary lanes (types, source lints) are excluded from Buildkite and run in GitHub Actions instead.

claims.claim: There are 2,149 test files under `test/`, distributed as `test/js` 1,307, `test/regression` 426, `test/cli` 202, `test/bundler` 110, `test/napi` 60, `test/internal` 57, `test/integration` 28, `test/bake` 27, and `test/v8` 1.

`scripts/runner.node.ts` is explicitly documented as running each `bun test` invocation in a separate process to catch crashes, as unable to use Bun APIs (it runs under Node), and as importing no dependencies so it starts fast.

`test/harness.ts` (2,367 lines) is the shared fixture layer, exporting `bunExe()`, `bunEnv`, `tempDir`/`tempDirWithFiles`, `normalizeBunSnapshot`, platform predicates (`isMacOS`, `isMusl`, `isASAN`, `isDebug`), `describeWithContainer` for Docker-backed suites, `getFDCount`, and RSS-delta assertions for leak tests.
Bundler tests use a purpose-built `itBundled` helper in `test/bundler/expectBundled.ts` rather than raw spawns, and the repo documents it as the required entry point for bundler/transpiler tests.

Regression tests are namespaced by real GitHub issue number under `test/regression/issue/`, and CLAUDE.md restricts that directory to true regressions — behavior that worked in a prior release — with everything else going into the existing module test file.

`test/internal/` tests the build system itself rather than the runtime — `build-rust-toolchain-probe.test.ts`, `build-post-link-ordering.test.ts`, `build-timings.test.ts`, `rust-check-all.test.ts`, `runner-junit.test.ts`, `parallel-allowlist.test.ts`.

Rust unit-test coverage is sparse relative to the surface: only 76 files under `src/` contain a `#[test]` attribute and 79 contain a `#[cfg(test)]` module, against ~701 Rust source files — correctness is overwhelmingly asserted from the JS side against a built binary.
CI test steps are sharded by platform — `parallelism` 20 on Linux, 8 on Windows, 2 on macOS, and 1 on the beta tier — with timeouts of 30/45/60 minutes and `soft_fail` only on the beta lane.

The Buildkite test step explicitly excludes `integration/bun-types` and `internal/source-lints`, delegating them to `.github/workflows/bun-types.yml` and `.github/workflows/source-lints.yml` because they never touch the built binary.

CI test jobs set `ASAN_OPTIONS=allow_user_segv_handler=1:disable_coredump=0:detect_leaks=0` and assert the agent's actual platform via `EXPECTED_PLATFORM_OS`/`ARCH`/`ABI`/`DISTRO`/`RELEASE` before running any test, so a mislabeled agent fails loudly instead of silently testing the wrong target.

Leak testing has dedicated infrastructure: a `testleak` npm script that enables `BUN_DESTRUCT_VM_ON_EXIT=1` with LSAN suppressions from `test/leaksan.supp`, plus in-binary suppressions compiled into `__lsan_default_suppressions` for Rust-side structural allocations.

Flakiness and timing are managed as tracked data files rather than ad-hoc retries: `test/flaky-tests.txt`, `test/expected-durations.json`, `test/parallel-allowlist.json`, `test/parallel-denylist.txt`, and `test/expectations.txt`.

The test workspace pulls in ~100 real npm packages (express, fastify, nest, prisma, typeorm, mongodb, socket.io, webpack, astro, svelte, verdaccio, vitest) so compatibility is asserted against actual ecosystem code rather than mocks.
The documented verification contract for a new test is dual-run: it must fail under `USE_SYSTEM_BUN=1 bun test <file>` and pass under `bun bd test <file>`, otherwise the test is considered invalid.
Test-failure triage is tooled: `bun run ci:errors`, `ci:status`, `ci:logs`, `ci:watch`, and `ci:slowest` wrap the BuildKite CLI through `scripts/find-build.ts` and `scripts/ci-slowest-tests.ts`.

risk_map.summary: The dominant risk class is memory safety across a Rust/C++/JSC boundary where `unsafe` is routine, raw pointers are stored across event-loop turns, and GC interaction is manual — `REVIEW.md` names this the most-blocked review category. Security-sensitive paths include registry credential handling, lifecycle scripts and the out-of-process security scanner, runtime C compilation via TinyCC, `Bun.secrets` keychain access, S3 SigV4 signing, CSRF token HMACs, the dev server's Host-header check, and the self-upgrade download path. Fragile coupling shows up where a value must stay in sync with an out-of-repo consumer (crash-report tag chars and `bun.report`) or with generated code. Blast-radius hotspots are the very large single files: `bundle_v2.rs` (8,079 lines), `VirtualMachine.rs` (7,700), `DevServer.rs` (6,792), `RequestContext.rs` (4,794), `server/mod.rs` (4,372).

claims.claim: `Run::start` holds the JSC API lock in a guard that is never dropped, justified only by the function's `-> !` return type — any future refactor that makes it return would leak or double-release the lock.

The run path deliberately leaks the entry path (`Box::leak(entry_path)`) because `vm.main` stores a raw backref into it and the hot reloader also retains it; correctness depends on the process never unwinding out of `start()`.

CPU/heap profiler config casts `ctx`-owned `Box<[u8]>` borrows to `'static` through `std::ptr::from_ref`, relying on the context being process-lifetime — a lifetime erasure that is correct only for this one caller.

`Tag::char()` must stay byte-for-byte in sync with a decoder in a separate repository (`oven-sh/bun.report`), and the comment pins a specific commit URL — a silent cross-repo coupling where adding a command breaks crash-report demangling with no local test.

Crash reports are uploaded to a default remote base URL (`https://bun.report`) encoding the command tag, platform, and address trace; there is an override and a disable path, but the default is outbound network on crash.

Registry credentials are parsed from `_authToken` segments and from bunfig scope objects into a single `NpmRegistry` value, meaning a bunfig or `.npmrc` parsing bug is directly a credential-disclosure or credential-confusion risk across registries.

`bun install` executes arbitrary package-authored lifecycle scripts via `bun_spawn`, gated by a `trustedDependencies` allowlist plus a checked-in `default-trusted-dependencies.txt` — the allowlist is the only thing between an install and arbitrary code execution.

The security scanner runs third-party scanner modules in a child process communicating over fds 3 and 4; the child reads the packages JSON to EOF and a write failure only prints to stderr and exits 1, so protocol-level failures depend on the parent correctly distinguishing scan failure from clean scan.

`bun:ffi` compiles and executes attacker-influenced C at runtime through a vendored TinyCC fork, and `dlopen`s arbitrary shared libraries — an intentional capability with no sandbox, so any path that lets untrusted input reach `Bun.FFI.cc` is a full compromise.

`bun upgrade` downloads release tarballs from GitHub, verifies a `sha256:` digest only when `version.digest.tag.is_supported()`, and additionally shells out to an external verify step — so an unsupported digest tag silently degrades integrity checking to whatever the verify subprocess does.

The dev server's `is_allowed_host_header` allows any bare IP literal as a Host value; combined with binding to a non-loopback address this widens the accepted origin set beyond the configured hostname.

CSRF tokens are HMAC-signed with a caller-supplied secret and an optional `session_id`; an empty `session_id` slice explicitly means the token is bound to no principal, so a caller omitting it produces tokens valid for any session.
Analytics are on by default and gated by a `TriState` plus the `DO_NOT_TRACK` env var, with a packed feature bitset recording which APIs a run touched — telemetry that is opt-out rather than opt-in.

Five files exceed 4,000 lines and concentrate blast radius: `bundle_v2.rs` (8,079), `VirtualMachine.rs` (7,700), `DevServer.rs` (6,792), `RequestContext.rs` (4,794), and `server/mod.rs` (4,372); a change in any one touches most of a subsystem's invariants at once.

`RequestContext` cannot express its transport type through Rust's type system (the handle type varies with `(ssl_enabled, http3)` and stable Rust can't drive an associated type from a const-generic bool), and the file documents an abandoned trait-based approach — a known-fragile generic design that future transports must work around.

Dead code is policed by an external cross-crate analyzer (`hawk.toml`) configured to union reachability across all 11 shipped targets through a throwaway `bun_hawk_root` binary, implying ordinary `cargo` dead-code lints do not catch unreachable code in this workspace.

extension_points.summary: Extension happens at five layers. New CLI subcommands add a `Tag` variant plus a dispatch arm and an out-lined `#[cold]` body. New JS classes are declared in `*.classes.ts` and generated into paired Rust/C++ bindings, or hand-written as the three-class JSC pattern. The `Bun` global is a static hash table in `BunObject.cpp` — adding a property is a table row plus a callback. Userland extends the bundler and runtime through `Bun.plugin` (regex-filter groups of onResolve/onLoad callbacks) and native plugins via `packages/bun-native-plugin-rs`/`-api`. Frameworks extend Bake through `FrameworkRouter` and the `UserOptions` framework description. The install path is extensible through a user-supplied security scanner module and bunfig-declared registries and scopes.

claims.claim: Adding a CLI command means adding a `Tag` variant, a unique crash-report `char()`, an arm in `Command::start`'s match, and an out-lined `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` exec fn — the file documents this convention so `start` stays a jump table.

Package-manager commands are registered through a macro table mapping an exec fn to a `(Tag, handler)` pair — `exec_install => (InstallCommand, InstallCommand::exec)` and seventeen siblings — so new pm verbs plug into one list.

New JS-visible classes are declared in a `.classes.ts` file (`define({ name, proto, values, JSType })`) and `src/codegen/generate-classes.ts` emits the prototype, constructor, subspace, and Rust binding — ~25 such definitions exist under `src/runtime/api/` alone.

Properties on the `Bun` global are added as rows in the `BunObject.cpp` static hash table, choosing between `Function`, `PropertyCallback` (lazily constructed), and `CustomAccessor` — no separate registration call is needed.

`Bun.plugin` is implemented as `Zig::BunPlugin` holding `Group`s of JIT-compiled `JSC::RegExp` filters paired with JS callbacks plus a `VirtualModuleMap`, targeted per `BunPluginTarget` — that is the userland hook for onResolve/onLoad.
Native (non-JS) bundler plugins are a supported extension surface with published scaffolding: a C API in `packages/bun-native-bundler-plugin-api` and a Rust crate in `packages/bun-native-plugin-rs`.

Bake is explicitly designed as framework infrastructure rather than a framework, with `UserOptions`/`Framework` parsed `from_js` in `bake_body.rs` and routing delegated to a pluggable `FrameworkRouter` keyed by `OpaqueFileId`.

Reference framework integrations ship in-tree as plugin packages — `packages/bun-plugin-svelte`, `packages/bun-plugin-yaml`, and `src/runtime/bake/bun-framework-react` — which double as the worked examples for third parties.

`bun install` accepts a user-supplied security scanner module: `scanner-entry.ts` is templated with `__SCANNER_MODULE__`/`__SUPPRESS_ERROR__`, runs the module in a child process, and returns typed `Bun.Security.Advisory[]` results.

Registries and per-scope credentials are declarative extension points in `bunfig.toml` — `[install]` `registry` and `[install.scopes]` entries each parse into an `api::NpmRegistry` accepting either a URL string or an object with `url`/`username`/`password`/`token`.

Node module surface is extended by adding a TypeScript file under `src/js/node/` and, when native work is needed, a paired binding in `src/runtime/node/*_binding.rs`; the bundler picks new modules up through `internal-module-registry-scanner.ts`.

Host functions callable from bundled JS are registered through `js2native` codegen: `$rust(ffi.rs, Bun__FFI__cc)` resolves to a Rust path derived from the file basename, which is why `ffi/mod.rs` re-exports `bun__ffi__cc` under a codegen-expected module path.

Loader/target behavior is extended through `src/options_types/` (`Loader`, `Target`, `api::Target`) rather than by branching in callers, and lower crates switch on `command_tag::Tag` without importing the CLI crate.

Compile-time string→value tables are generated from `*.string-map.ts` files into `*.generated.rs` via `bun run codegen:string-maps`, with a `codegen:verify` script that fails CI if the generated output is stale.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `CLAUDE.md`, `REVIEW.md`, `src/AGENTS.md`, and `src/js/AGENTS.md` before writing anything — they encode rules that are enforced, not suggestions. The single most important operational fact: never run `bun test` or `bun <file>` directly; use `bun bd` (which builds the debug binary and execs it with trailing args) so your native changes are actually exercised. Prefer in-tree helpers over `std` — `clippy.toml` mechanically bans `std::fs::*`, `std::env::var`, `std::thread::spawn`, and `std::mem::zeroed`. Add tests to the existing file for the module you changed, not a new file, and reserve `test/regression/issue/<n>.test.ts` for real regressions with a real issue number. Branch names must start with `claude/`. The one documented exception to the build requirement is `packages/bun-types/**/*.d.ts`, which can be tested with the system Bun.

claims.claim: Build and run with `bun bd` — it builds the debug binary and passes trailing args through to it; `bun bd test <file>` is the only valid way to run tests against your changes, and `bun bd` must not be given a timeout.

Every build script supports build-then-exec with the same arg routing: build flags first, then the first unrecognized arg (or an explicit `--`) starts the exec args, and build output is suppressed unless the build fails.

`clippy.toml` is a hard boundary: it lists disallowed methods with replacement guidance — `std::fs::*` → `bun_sys::file`/`dir`, `std::env::var` → `bun_core::env_var`, `std::thread::spawn` → `bun_threading::spawn_named`, `std::mem::zeroed` → `MaybeUninit` (zeroed is UB for most Bun types).

Error handling follows a fixed shape: each crate defines a `thiserror` enum at `<crate>/error.rs` re-exported as `crate::Error`/`crate::Result`; the syscall boundary uses `bun_sys::Maybe<T>`; OOM routes through `bun_alloc::AllocError`; and `.unwrap()` is only for invariants you can prove, never for anything user input or the OS can reach.

`mordant.toml` runs a ratcheting Rust lint pass against `mordant-baseline.toml`: a PR fails only when it adds a new finding for an existing (lint, file) pair, so expect to either fix or regenerate the baseline via `bun run rust:mordant:baseline`.

Platform-gated code is not type-checked unless that target is built — run `bun run rust:check-all` (which drives `scripts/rust-check-all.ts` across linux/macos/windows × x64/aarch64) after touching any `#[cfg(...)]` branch.

Built-in JS in `src/js/` must be tamper-resistant: `$`-prefixed intrinsics and primordial-safe calls (`$isJSArray`, `map.$get`, `$call`), globals captured at module load, `node:`-prefixed requires, and never routing internal logic through user-overridable machinery like `Array.isArray`.

Tests must copy harness conventions exactly: `tempDir` from `"harness"` (never `tmpdirSync` or `fs.mkdtempSync`), `port: 0` always, `normalizeBunSnapshot` for snapshot output, `Promise.all` to drain stdout/stderr/exited concurrently, and stdout assertions before the exit-code assertion.

Never use `setTimeout`/`sleep` to wait for a condition in a test — poll with a deadline or await the event; reviewers treat a bare sleep of 50ms or more outside a bounded poll loop as requiring a comment naming why no observable signal exists.

The single most-repeated trap in this repo's instructions: the JSC conservative stack scanner is never the cause of a bug you are debugging; a surviving object is held by a real reference, and blaming the scanner requires a heap snapshot plus a debugger session as PR artifacts.

Arena allocation is a known memory trap: values in a `bumpalo`/`Arena` do not run `Drop` on reset, so anything owning a heap allocation or refcount must be freed explicitly first, mirroring the original Zig `deinit()` ordering.

Verify exception-check correctness with `BUN_JSC_validateExceptionChecks=1 BUN_JSC_dumpSimulatedThrows=1 bun bd <command>` rather than adding suppression-list entries, and silence debug logging with `BUN_DEBUG_QUIET_LOGS=1` or enable one scope with `BUN_DEBUG_<SCOPE>=1`.

PR feedback is read with `bun run pr:comments` (which paginates past 100 and filters bot noise) rather than `gh`, and CI failures with `bun run ci:errors` / `ci:status` / `ci:logs`, which wrap the BuildKite CLI via `scripts/find-build.ts`.

Situational review rules are deliberately kept out of the main file: `.claude/docs/landing-prs.md` holds the Node/Web-compat, API-design, performance, cross-platform, vendoring, docs/types, and PR-process sections, to be read before the work each covers.

Repo-specific skills exist for the recurring hard tasks and should be preferred over improvising: implementing JSC classes in C++ or Rust, the JSC garbage-collector reference, `bun_sys` system calls, and writing bundler and dev-server tests.

readmePreview: | | | | \| | / | | | | |) | | | (| || | <| | \|\/|| \\| README Curl is a command line tool for transferring data specified with URL syntax.

overview.summary: This is the curl project at 8.23.0-DEV: a C89-portable transfer library (libcurl, `lib/`, ~393 files) plus the `curl` command-line tool (`src/`, ~96 files) that is a thin client of that library. libcurl speaks ~25 URI schemes (HTTP/1-2-3, FTP(S), SMTP/IMAP/POP3, SCP/SFTP, LDAP, MQTT, RTSP, TFTP, DICT, Gopher, Telnet, WS(S), file) through a scheme registry of `struct Curl_scheme` records, and layers transport concerns (happy-eyeballs, SOCKS, HTTP proxy, HAProxy, TLS, QUIC, HTTP/2) as a stackable chain of connection filters rather than protocol-specific socket code. What is distinctive is the amount of pluggability compiled in: six TLS backends, two QUIC backends, two SSH backends, three DNS resolver strategies, ~50 `CURL_DISABLE_*` build knobs, and a ~2,100-case integration test suite driven by in-tree protocol servers. The audience is everyone from distro maintainers embedding libcurl to contributors adding a protocol or a command-line option.

system_map.summary: Two build artefacts share one repo: `lib/` builds libcurl, `src/` builds the `curl` tool on top of the public headers in `include/curl/`. The tool owns argv parsing, output files, globbing and retries; libcurl owns URL parsing, connection reuse, the multi state machine, and the filter chain that actually moves bytes. Backends live in `lib/vtls` (TLS), `lib/vquic` (QUIC/HTTP3), `lib/vssh` (SCP/SFTP), `lib/vauth` (SASL/NTLM/Kerberos), `lib/vdns` (resolvers + DoH), with `lib/curlx/` as the portability/utility layer shared by both. There is no database — persistence is flat files (cookie jar, HSTS, alt-svc, TLS session cache) plus whatever the user redirects output to. Two parallel build systems (autotools via `configure.ac`/`Makefile.am` and CMake via a 93KB `CMakeLists.txt`) are both first-class and CI-verified against each other.

claims.claim: The CLI process entrypoint is `main()` in src/tool_main.c, which runs `tool_init_stderr()`, `main_checkfds()` (reopens fds 0/1/2 on /dev/null so sockets can never land on stdin/stdout/stderr), ignores SIGPIPE, then calls `globalconf_init()` → `operate(argc, argv)` → `globalconf_free()`.

`operate()` is the tool's real driver: it forces `LC_NUMERIC=C`, reads `.curlrc` via `parseconfig()` unless argv[1] is `-q`/`--disable`, calls `parse_args()`, creates one `CURLSH` share handle, then hands off to `run_all_transfers()`.

The public API surface is 12 headers under include/curl/ — `curl.h` (options/CURLcode), `multi.h`, `easy.h`, `urlapi.h`, `websockets.h`, `header.h`, `options.h`, `mprintf.h`, `system.h`, `curlver.h` — and `curlver.h` pins this tree at LIBCURL_VERSION "8.23.0-DEV" / LIBCURL_VERSION_NUM 0x081700.

Every URI scheme libcurl knows is a `const struct Curl_scheme` (name, `run` vtable pointer, protocol bit, family bit, PROTOPT_* flags, default port) defined in lib/protocol.c and externed in lib/protocol.h; a scheme compiled out (e.g. `CURL_DISABLE_FTP`) keeps its record but gets a `ZERO_NULL` `run` pointer.

Scheme lookup avoids a linear table scan: `Curl_getn_scheme()` dispatches on name length into `two_letter_scheme()` … `seven_letter_scheme()`, each a hand-written switch on the first character, and rejects any name shorter than 2 or longer than 7 characters.

Transport is a chain of connection filters: `struct Curl_cftype` supplies do_connect/do_send/do_recv/do_shutdown/adjust_pollset/query, and `struct Curl_cfilter` links instances via `->next`, so TLS writes into whatever is below it without knowing whether that is a socket, a proxy tunnel, or HTTP/2.

Concrete filter types are registered as `struct Curl_cftype Curl_cft_*` across the tree: tcp/udp/unix/tcp_accept (lib/cf-socket.c), ip_happy, socks_proxy, http_proxy, h1/h2 proxy, haproxy, http_connect, nghttp2, http3 (both ngtcp2 and quiche), capsule, dns, and recvbuf.

The runtime boundary between easy and multi is one-way: the multi interface is the engine and `curl_easy_perform()` is a wrapper that creates (and caches on `data->multi_easy`) a 1-handle multi and pumps it.

Each transfer is a 16-state machine (`MSTATE_INIT` … `MSTATE_MSGSENT`) declared in lib/multihandle.h and driven by `multi_runsingle()` in lib/multi.c, which is 4,262 lines and the single busiest file in the library.

TLS is selected from a compile-ordered array `available_backends[]` (wolfSSL, GnuTLS, mbedTLS, OpenSSL, Schannel, Rustls); `CURL_SSL_BACKEND` in the environment can pick among them at runtime when multiple are built in.

The storage layer is plain files, not a database: cookie jars via `cookie_output()`/`Curl_flush_cookies()`, HSTS via `Curl_hsts_save()`, Alt-Svc via `Curl_altsvc_save()`, and TLS session blobs via `tool_ssls_save()` called from `operate()`.

Build/test commands live in the top Makefile.am: `make check` = test + examples + check-docs; `make test`, `test-full`, `test-nonflaky`, `test-torture`, `test-event`, `test-ci`, `pytest`; plus `make checksrc`, `make badwords`, `make lint`, `make tidy`, and `make ca-bundle`.

CI is spread over 15 GitHub Actions workflows (linux, linux-old, macos, windows, non-native, http3-linux, distcheck, codeql, checksrc, checkdocs, checkurls, configure-vs-cmake, curl-for-win, appveyor-status, label), with AppVeyor and CircleCI configs alongside; dependency versions are pinned in workflow `env:` and bumped by Renovate.

The Dockerfile is not a deployment artefact — it is a pinned-digest debian:bookworm-slim reproducible *release* environment, used to run `autoreconf`, `configure`, `make`, and `scripts/maketgz` with a fixed `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`.

`lib/curlx/` is a deliberately separate portability layer (dynbuf, strparse, base64, inet_pton/ntop, timeval, nonblock, multibyte, win32-fopen, warnless) that both `lib/` and `src/` link, which is why tool code calls `curlx_*` rather than libc directly.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface splits in two. The `curl` tool exposes ~298 documented command-line options plus higher-level conveniences: URL globbing, parallel transfers, retry policies, ETag compare/store, `--write-out` templating (including JSON), config files, user-defined `--variable` expansion, `--libcurl` source generation, and xattr metadata. libcurl exposes ~91 documented API functions and ~422 documented options, covering the easy, multi, share, URL, header, mime, and WebSocket APIs. Protocol coverage is the headline feature: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, FTP(S), SFTP/SCP, SMTP/IMAP/POP3, LDAP(S), MQTT, RTSP, TFTP, DICT, Gopher, Telnet, WS(S), and local `file`. Authentication and proxying are each their own subsystem with many interchangeable mechanisms.

claims.claim: The command-line grammar is a single alphabetically-sorted `aliases[]` table of `struct LongShort` (long name, ARG_* type bits such as ARG_BOOL/ARG_FILE/ARG_STRG/ARG_SECS plus ARG_NO/ARG_TLS/ARG_CLEAR modifiers, short letter, and a `C_*` id); `findlongopt()`/`findshortopt()` resolve into it.

Every command-line option has a matching curldown page — 298 files under docs/cmdline-opts/ — and the underscore-prefixed ones (`_OPTIONS.md`, `_GLOBBING.md`, `_VARIABLES.md`, `_EXITCODES.md`) are the manpage's prose sections.

`--parallel` switches the tool from `serial_transfers()` to `parallel_transfers()`, which drives a real `CURLM` with `CURLMOPT_MAX_HOST_CONNECTIONS`, a notify callback, and `curl_multi_poll()`/`curl_multi_perform()`; concurrency is capped by `MAX_PARALLEL`/`MAX_PARALLEL_HOST` with `PARALLEL_DEFAULT` as the default.
URL globbing (`http://host/[1-100]`, `{a,b}`) is implemented in src/tool_urlglob.c and feeds `glob_match_url()`, which also resolves `#1`..`#9` back-references when composing output filenames.

`--write-out` is table-driven: a `writeoutvar variables[]` array maps names like `http_code`, `time_total`, `num_retries`, `conn_id`, `filename_effective` to a CURLINFO id and a writer function, with `%{json}`, `%{header_json}`, `%header{}`, `%time{}` and `%output{}` handled as special forms.

`--libcurl <file>` makes the tool emit an equivalent C program: `easysrc_init()`/`easysrc_perform()`/`dumpeasysrc()` are wired into `operate()` and the serial loop, and the `my_setopt*` macros in src/tool_setopt.c double as source emitters.
`--variable` supports environment expansion with functions: src/var.c reads `getenv(name)` directly (rather than `curl_getenv()`) specifically so that a blank-but-set variable is distinguishable.
IPFS/IPNS URLs are a tool-level feature that reads `IPFS_GATEWAY`, then falls back to `IPFS_PATH`, then `$HOME/.ipfs/gateway`, rewriting `ipfs://` into an HTTP gateway request.

Transfer resilience is a tool feature, not a library one: `retrycheck()` retries on timeouts/resolve failures, on HTTP 408/429/500/502/503/504/522/524, on FTP 4xx, on `--retry-connrefused`, and on `--retry-all-errors`, truncating the output file before each new attempt.

HTTP/3 ships with two interchangeable QUIC backends — ngtcp2 (`lib/vquic/cf-ngtcp2.c`) and quiche (`lib/vquic/cf-quiche.c`) — each registering a `Curl_cft_http3` filter, plus an experimental HTTP/3 proxy path via `cf-ngtcp2-proxy.c` and CONNECT-UDP capsules.
WebSocket support is a public API (`curl_ws_recv()`, `curl_ws_send()`, `curl_ws_meta()`) declared in include/curl/websockets.h and implemented in lib/ws.c with frame-level fragmentation handling.

Authentication mechanisms are pluggable per-mechanism files under lib/vauth/: cleartext, CRAM-MD5, DIGEST (native and SSPI), NTLM (native and SSPI), Kerberos 5 (GSSAPI and SSPI), SPNEGO (GSSAPI and SSPI), OAuth2, and GSASL.

Request signing is supported for two schemes: AWS SigV4 (`lib/http_aws_sigv4.c`, `--aws-sigv4`) and HTTP Message Signatures (`lib/http_httpsig.c`, wired through `httpsig_setopts()` with `CURLOPT_HTTPSIG_ALGORITHM`/`CURLOPT_HTTPSIG_KEY`).

DNS-over-HTTPS is implemented as sub-transfers: `Curl_doh()` spins up to three probes (A, AAAA, HTTPS RR) as separate easy handles attached to the parent via `CURL_EZM_DOH_PROBE` metadata and a `sub_xfer_done` callback.

Proxy support spans SOCKS4/4a/5/5h (`lib/socks.c` plus GSSAPI/SSPI variants), HTTP proxies with CONNECT tunneling over HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (`lib/cf-h1-proxy.c`, `lib/cf-h2-proxy.c`), and the HAProxy PROXY protocol header (`lib/cf-haproxy.c`).

data_flow.summary: Input boundaries are argv, `.curlrc`/`-K` config files, environment variables, `.netrc`, stdin uploads, and the network. argv is normalised into a linked list of `struct OperationConfig` (one per `--next`), which `config2setopts.c` translates wholesale into `curl_easy_setopt()` calls; from there the state owner is `struct Curl_easy` (`data->set` for user intent, `data->state`/`data->req` for per-request state). The URL becomes a `CURLU` via lib/urlapi.c, resolves to a `struct Curl_scheme`, and is matched against the connection pool before a filter chain is built. Bytes in from the network flow up through `Curl_xfer_write_resp()` → `Curl_client_write()` → an ordered writer stack → `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION`; bytes out flow down through the mirror-image client reader chain. Output boundaries are the write callbacks (which the tool points at files or stdout), the header callback, the progress callback, and the file-backed caches flushed at cleanup.

claims.claim: argv is consumed by `parse_args()`, which loops over argv, calls `getparameter()` per flag, treats bare arguments as `--url`, and on `PARAM_NEXT_OPERATION` allocates a fresh `OperationConfig` and links it onto `global->last` — so `--next` literally forks the config list.

Config files are a second input boundary parsed by the same code path: `operate()` calls `parseconfig(NULL, CONFIG_MAX_LEVELS, &curlrc_path)` for `.curlrc` before argv, and `-K` re-enters it, with recursion bounded by `CONFIG_MAX_LEVELS`.

The config→library translation is centralised in src/config2setopts.c, split into `ssh_setopts()`, `ssl_ca_setopts()`, `ssl_setopts()`, `cookie_setopts()`, `httpsig_setopts()`, `http_setopts()` and friends, all using `my_setopt_*` wrappers so the same call sites feed both libcurl and the `--libcurl` code generator.

Library-side, options land in `struct Curl_easy` guarded by `magic == CURLEASY_MAGIC_NUMBER`; `lib/setopt.c` fans out into typed setters (`setopt_long_bool`, `setopt_long_net`, `setopt_long_ssl`, `setopt_long_proxy`, `setopt_long_http`) rather than one giant switch.

URLs are parsed by `parseurl()` in lib/urlapi.c into a `CURLU`, with behaviour gated by flags such as `CURLU_GUESS_SCHEME`, `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME`, `CURLU_NO_AUTHORITY`, `CURLU_DISALLOW_USER`, `CURLU_URLENCODE` and `CURLU_PATH_AS_IS`; the same parser backs the public `curl_url_*` API.

The parsed scheme is only accepted for a connection if it passes `url_set_conn_scheme()`, which requires a non-NULL `run` vtable and membership in `data->set.allowed_protocols` (and `redir_protocols` when following a redirect) — this is the choke point that makes `--proto`/`--proto-redir` effective.

Before dialling out, libcurl asks the connection pool for a reusable `connectdata` through `Curl_cpool_find()` with a match callback; reuse eligibility consults PROTOPT_SSL/PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE/PROTOPT_CONN_REUSE and compares origins and protocol families.

Received bytes enter the client-writer chain via `Curl_client_write()`, which lazily builds the stack (`Curl_cwt_out` at CURL_CW_CLIENT, `cw_download` at CURL_CW_PROTOCOL, `cw_raw` at CURL_CW_RAW) and inserts each new writer first within its phase.

Writer ordering is a fixed phase enum — RAW → TRANSFER_DECODE → PROTOCOL → BEFORE_DECODE → CONTENT_DECODE → CLIENT — so chunked decoding, size accounting, and gzip/brotli/zstd decompression always run in that order before the application callback.

`cw_download_write()` is where `--max-filesize` is enforced and where excess body bytes beyond `req.maxdownload` cause `connclose()`; exceeding the limit returns `CURLE_FILESIZE_EXCEEDED` from inside the writer chain.

Upload data flows through the mirror-image client-reader chain with phases CLIENT → CONTENT_ENCODE → PROTOCOL → TRANSFER_ENCODE → NET, entered via `Curl_client_read()`; HTTP's Expect: 100-continue is itself implemented as a reader (`cr_exp100_read`).

On the tool side the terminal output boundary is `tool_cb_wrt.c`'s write callback writing into a `struct OutStruct` (stream, filename, `fopened`, `init` offset), with `setup_outfile()` deciding stdout vs. file vs. `--out-null` and opening in append mode when resuming.

Response headers reach the tool through `tool_cb_hdr.c`, where `parse_filename()` derives a local name from `Content-Disposition:` (or `Location:`) by trimming quotes, query/fragment, CR/LF, and any path prefix before `/` or `\`.

Cross-transfer state is shared deliberately: `share_setup()` enables `CURL_LOCK_DATA_COOKIE`, `DNS`, `SSL_SESSION`, `PSL`, `HSTS` on the `CURLSH`, and adds `CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT` only in serial mode because parallel mode uses the multi handle's own pool.

Persistence is flushed at teardown rather than continuously: `Curl_flush_cookies()` writes the jar through `cookie_output()`, and `Curl_fopen()` performs the durable write as O_EXCL temp file + `fchmod` clone of the original mode + rename.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows explain most of the codebase: tool startup, a single serial transfer, and the multi state machine that both serial and parallel modes ultimately run on. The tool never calls sockets directly — it builds `per_transfer` records, sets options, and calls `curl_easy_perform()` (serial) or feeds a `CURLM` (parallel). Inside libcurl, `curl_easy_perform()` is itself a multi loop, so every transfer walks `MSTATE_INIT` → … → `MSTATE_MSGSENT` in `multi_runsingle()`. Connection establishment is a re-entrant loop inside one filter (`cf_setup_connect`) that appends the next filter and restarts the sub-chain connect until the whole stack is up.

claims.claim: STARTUP: `main()` → `tool_init_stderr()` → (Windows only) `win32_init()` → `main_checkfds()` → `signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN)` → `memory_tracking_init()` (reads `CURL_MEMDEBUG`/`CURL_MEMLIMIT` on debug builds) → `globalconf_init()` → `operate()` → `globalconf_free()`.

STARTUP (cont.): inside `operate()` the order is `setlocale(LC_NUMERIC,"C")` → `parseconfig()` for `.curlrc` → `parse_args()` → `easysrc_init()` if `--libcurl` → `curl_share_init()` → `share_setup()` → `tool_ssls_load()` → `get_args()` per OperationConfig → `run_all_transfers()` → `curl_share_cleanup()` → `dumpeasysrc()` → `varcleanup()`.

PRIMARY ACTION (serial): `run_all_transfers()` → `serial_transfers()` → `create_transfer()` → `transfer_per_config()` → `cacertpaths()` → `single_transfer()` → `create_single()`, then per item `pre_transfer()` → `curl_easy_perform()` → `post_per_transfer()`; a retry sleeps `curlx_wait_ms(delay_ms)` and re-runs the same `per`.

`create_single()` builds one `per_transfer` by walking `setup_input_file()` → `setup_url_pattern()` → `setup_etag_files()` → `curl_easy_init()` → `add_per_transfer()`, and only then applies output/header/option setup; failure paths must both `curl_easy_cleanup()` and close any opened etag stream.

`pre_transfer()` is what turns `-T file` into `CURLOPT_INFILESIZE_LARGE`: it opens the upload file with `curlx_open(O_RDONLY|CURL_O_BINARY)`, `fstat`s it, and deliberately skips the size for non-`S_ISREG` inputs (devices, sockets, FIFOs).

PRIMARY ACTION (parallel): `parallel_transfers()` → `curl_multi_init()` → set `CURLMOPT_QUICK_EXIT`, `CURLMOPT_NOTIFYFUNCTION=mnotify`, `CURLMOPT_MAX_HOST_CONNECTIONS` → `curl_multi_notify_enable(CURLMNOTIFY_INFO_READ)` → `add_parallel_transfers()` → loop { `curl_multi_poll(…,1000,…)`; `curl_multi_perform()`; `progress_meter()` } with completions harvested in `check_finished()`.

`--fail-early` and fatal errors are implemented as a cooperative abort: `check_finished()` sets `s->wrapitup`, the main loop then sets `per->abort = TRUE` on every added transfer, and the progress callback turns that into `CURLE_ABORTED_BY_CALLBACK` which is rewritten into a clearer errorbuffer message.

LIBRARY ENTRY: `curl_easy_perform()` → `CURL_EAPI_ENTER` guard → `easy_perform()`, which refuses a handle already in a user multi, detaches any connect-only connection, reuses or creates `data->multi_easy` via `Curl_multi_handle(16,1,3,7,3)`, copies MAXCONNECTS/QUICK_EXIT, `Curl_multi_add_handle()`, `sigpipe_init/apply`, then `easy_transfer()`.

`easy_transfer()` is the blocking pump: `curl_multi_poll()` → `curl_multi_perform()` → when `still_running` hits 0, `curl_multi_info_read()` yields the CURLcode; a CURLMcode is mapped to `CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY` or `CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT`.

STATE MACHINE: `multi_runsingle()` clears the handle's dirty bit, optionally runs `multi_schedule_pending()`, checks `multi_handle_timeout()`, then switches to `multistate_init/setup/connect/connecting/protoconnect/protoconnecting/do/doing/doing_more/did/ratelimiting/performing/done`, looping while any handler returns `CURLM_CALL_MULTI_PERFORM`.

State transitions run entry hooks from a fixed `state_enter[MSTATE_LAST]` table in `mstate()` — only CONNECT, DID, DONE and COMPLETED have hooks — and every transition is traced via `CURL_TRC_M(data, "-> [%s]")`, which is what `--trace-config multi` surfaces.

CONNECT: `cf_setup_connect()` is a re-entrant loop that connects the sub-chain, then appends filters in a fixed order — ip_happy (happy eyeballs) → SOCKS → HTTP proxy → HAProxy → origin filters (TLS/ALPN) — restarting at `connect_sub_chain` after each addition until `CF_SETUP_DONE`.

The multi handle's `admin` easy handle is a special case in `multi_runsingle()`: it consumes internal wakeups, drives `Curl_async_thrdd_multi_process()` for threaded resolution, and runs `Curl_cshutdn_perform()` for graceful connection shutdowns, then returns early.

PERSISTENCE: at the end of `operate()`, if `--ssl-sessions` and the `ssls_export` feature are present, `tool_ssls_save()` writes the TLS session cache back out; cookie jars are written from libcurl's own cleanup path via `Curl_flush_cookies()`.

TEARDOWN: `run_all_transfers()` always drains the `transfers` list after the mode-specific loop, calling `post_per_transfer()` + `clean_getout()` + `del_per_transfer()` for each leftover, and restores the saved `global->noprogress`/`global->isatty`.

testing_signals.summary: curl's testing is unusually broad and almost entirely in-tree. The centre of gravity is `tests/data/` — 2,119 XML-ish test-case files run by `tests/runtests.pl` against protocol servers curl itself ships (sws, socksd, tftpd, mqttd, rtspd, dnsd, plus Perl/Python FTP/TFTP/RTSP/DICT/telnet servers). Around that sit 80 C unit tests for library internals, 6 `tunit` tests for tool-only code, 273 `libtest` programs exercising the public API, and 31 pytest modules that test HTTP/2, HTTP/3, proxying, SSL and WebSockets against real nghttpx/caddy/vsftpd. Each run can be repeated in torture mode (fail every allocation in turn), under valgrind, or event-based. Coverage gaps are structural rather than accidental: platform-specific code (Windows/VMS/AmigaOS/MSDOS branches) and the rarer TLS/QUIC backend combinations can only be exercised by the matching CI job.

claims.claim: The primary suite is 2,119 declarative test files in tests/data/, each an XML-like document with `<info><keywords>`, a `<reply>` server script, a `<client><command>` invocation, and a `<verify><protocol>` expectation — plus optional `<limits>` on allocation counts.

`tests/runtests.pl` is the harness; its documented flags cover torture testing (`-t`), valgrind control, event-based runs, and keyword/feature selection such as `FTPS` or `!feat:proxy`, with per-test result flags (s/r/p/d/u/P/o/e/m/v/E) reported per run.

Protocol servers are part of the repo, so tests need no external services: tests/server/ holds sws.c (HTTP), socksd.c, tftpd.c, mqttd.c, rtspd.c, dnsd.c and sockfilt.c, complemented by ftpserver.pl, http2-server.pl, http3-server.pl, sshserver.pl and dictserver.py.

80 unit tests under tests/unit/ exercise library internals directly (llist, hash, splay, strparse, urlapi, cookie parsing …) using the `UNITTEST_BEGIN_SIMPLE` macro and a `test_unitNNNN(const char *arg)` entrypoint.

Tool-only code has its own unit directory, tests/tunit/, with 6 files named after the test number they back (tool1394, tool1604, tool1621, tool1622, tool1623, tool1720) — this is where `src/` helpers get direct coverage.

273 `libtest/libNNNN.c` programs plus a set of `cli_*.c` drivers (cli_h2_pausing, cli_hx_download, cli_ws_pingpong, cli_tls_session_reuse, cli_ev_download) test the public easy/multi/WebSocket APIs as real linked programs.

The pytest suite in tests/http/ has 31 modules numbered by area — 01 basic, 02 download, 07 upload, 09 push, 10/13 proxy and proxy auth, 17 ssl use, 19 shutdown, 20 websockets, 22 HTTPSRR, 30-32 vsftpd, 40 socks, 50/51 scp+sftp, 60 h3 proxy — driven by `conftest.py` and a `testenv` package.

Make targets select the mode: `tests/Makefile.am` maps `test`/`quiet-test`/`am-test`/`ci-test`/`full-test`/`nonflaky-test`/`torture-test`/`event-test` onto `$(TEST)` with different flag sets, and `ci-pytest` runs `pytest -n auto -v $(srcdir)/http`.

Memory-behaviour is a first-class test axis: debug builds honour `CURL_MEMDEBUG` (log file) and `CURL_MEMLIMIT` (fail the Nth allocation) set up in `memory_tracking_init()`, with tests/memanalyze.pl and tests/memanalyzer.pm analysing the logs and test cases asserting allocation ceilings.

Debug builds expose test-only hooks the suite depends on: `CURL_FORBID_REUSE`, `global->test_duphandle` (perform on a `curl_easy_duphandle()` copy), `global->test_event_based` (`curl_easy_perform_ev()` / libuv-driven `parallel_event()`), and `CURL_UPLOAD_SIZE`.

Source-level checks run as their own CI workflow: `scripts/checksrc-all.pl` enforces the style guide, and the same job runs spellcheck, `scripts/cmakeopts.sh`, REUSE licence checks and other linters with `permissions: {}` and pinned action SHAs.
Documentation is tested too: `make check` includes `check-docs` (docs/libcurl) and `examples` (docs/examples, 129 compilable C programs), with dedicated checkdocs.yml and checkurls.yml workflows.

The CI matrix is what covers the backend combinatorics: linux.yml pins and builds against AWS-LC, BoringSSL, LibreSSL, mbedTLS (current and previous), OpenSSL, Rustls, nghttp2, OpenLDAP and Fil-C, while http3-linux.yml, macos.yml, windows.yml, non-native.yml and linux-old.yml cover the rest.
There is a coverage script (`scripts/coverage.sh`) and a CodeQL workflow, but coverage is not gated in the in-tree build targets — `make check` does not compute or threshold line coverage.
`configure-vs-cmake.yml` exists specifically to catch drift between the two build systems, which is the main risk of maintaining `configure.ac` (167KB) and `CMakeLists.txt` (93KB) in parallel.

risk_map.summary: curl's risk profile is dominated by the fact that it parses hostile input (URLs, headers, server responses, redirect targets) in C, on every platform, across dozens of optional backends. The highest-attention paths are credential handling (.netrc, `-u`, redirects that must drop auth), filename derivation from server-controlled `Content-Disposition`, the redirect/protocol allowlist, and the TLS/QUIC backend glue. Structurally, the biggest fragility is combinatorial: ~50 `CURL_DISABLE_*` knobs times six TLS backends times two QUIC backends times platform `#ifdef`s means many buildable configurations that no single CI job exercises. Blast-radius hotspots are the few central files every protocol funnels through — lib/multi.c, lib/url.c, lib/sendf.c, lib/cfilters.c — where a regression is not protocol-local.

claims.claim: Server-controlled filenames reach the filesystem: `parse_filename()` in tool_cb_hdr.c strips path components and CR/LF, but the reserved-name / invalid-character sanitizer `sanitize_file_name()` is compiled only `#if defined(_WIN32) || defined(MSDOS)`, so POSIX hardening rests entirely on those `strrchr('/')`/`strrchr('\\')` trims.

`--output-dir` is applied by naive string concatenation (`curl_maprintf("%s/%s", config->output_dir, per->outfile)`) after the filename has been derived, so the safety of the combined path depends wholly on the earlier derivation step.

The protocol allowlist is enforced in exactly one place — `url_set_conn_scheme()` checking `data->set.allowed_protocols` and, for redirects, `data->set.redir_protocols` — making it a single point of failure for `--proto`/`--proto-redir` and for redirect-to-`file://` style attacks.

Credential-bearing code is spread across lib/creds.c, lib/netrc.c and lib/http.c's auth state machine (`Curl_http_output_auth`, `Curl_http_input_auth`, `http_perhapsrewind`, `Curl_http_auth_act`); the recent commit history shows this area actively hardened (e.g. keeping credentials out of `CURLINFO_REDIRECT_URL`).

.netrc parsing is a hand-written lexer over an attacker-influenceable file with explicit hard caps — `MAX_NETRC_LINE` 16384, `MAX_NETRC_FILE` 128KB, `MAX_NETRC_TOKEN` 4096 — and a quoted-string state machine (`netrc_lexer_quoted`) that is worth re-reading before any change.

Interactive password entry disables terminal echo by clearing the `ECHO` bit in `termios` and must restore it on every exit path; a failure here leaks a typed password to the screen and to scrollback.

Several environment variables change behaviour without any command-line trace: `IPFS_GATEWAY`/`IPFS_PATH`/`HOME` in the tool, and `CURL_SSL_BACKEND` inside libcurl, which selects among compiled-in TLS backends at runtime.

DoH creates additional easy handles that perform their own network transfers with their own option set (`ERROR_CHECK_SETOPT(CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION, doh_probe_write_cb)` etc.); any option not deliberately propagated to the probe is silently not applied to DNS traffic.

Explicitly-experimental surface is documented as out of scope for security handling: the quiche QUIC backend and HTTP/3 proxy / CONNECT-UDP support are experimental, and docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md states vulnerabilities in experimental features are treated as ordinary bugs.

Size is itself a risk in the hot files: lib/http.c is 5,112 lines, lib/multi.c 4,262, lib/ftp.c and lib/http2.c are next; `multi_runsingle()` alone dispatches thirteen states and is the path every protocol takes.

The `CURL_DISABLE_*` matrix (documented across ~50 entries in docs/CURL-DISABLE.md, from `CURL_DISABLE_ALTSVC` to `CURL_DISABLE_NETRC`) means many code paths are conditionally compiled; `scripts/randdisable` exists precisely because the full matrix cannot be CI-covered.

`Curl_fopen()` gets the durable-write pattern right (O_EXCL temp file, 0600, `fchmod` clone only when uid/gid match, then rename), so any new cache writer that bypasses it loses those properties — a coupling that is easy to miss.

Parallel mode's abort path is cooperative rather than immediate: `wrapitup` only sets `per->abort`, and the transfer does not stop until its progress callback next fires — so a stalled transfer can outlive a `--fail-early` decision.

The libuv-based event loop used by `--parallel` under `test_event_based` is `#if defined(DEBUGBUILD) && defined(USE_LIBUV)` only, so `parallel_event()`, `on_uv_socket()`, `cb_socket()` and `destroy_context()` are never exercised by a release build.

libcurl defends against API misuse at runtime rather than at compile time: magic-number checks (`CURLEASY_MAGIC_NUMBER`, `CURLMULTI_MAGIC_NUMBER`) and a call-stack guard that returns `CURLE_RECURSIVE_API_CALL` when an application re-enters the API from inside a callback.

extension_points.summary: curl is extended by adding a record to a table, not by subclassing. New URI schemes are `struct Curl_scheme` records pointing at a `struct Curl_protocol` vtable; new transport behaviour is a `struct Curl_cftype` inserted into the filter chain; new response processing is a `struct Curl_cwtype` registered at a phase; new TLS/SSH/DNS backends are entries in a backend array guarded by a `USE_*` define. On the tool side, a new command-line option means one row in the alphabetical `aliases[]` table, one `C_*` enum value, one case in `getparameter()`, and one curldown page. Several of these tables are additionally mirrored by generated files or documentation that CI verifies.

claims.claim: Adding a protocol means adding a `Curl_scheme_*` record in lib/protocol.c, externing it in lib/protocol.h, teaching the length-bucketed lookup functions about the new name, and supplying a `struct Curl_protocol` vtable; docs/internals/NEW-PROTOCOL.md documents the social and technical bar for that.

The `struct Curl_protocol` vtable is the per-scheme hook set: setup_connection, connect, connecting, do_it, doing, done, proto_getsock/doing_pollset/domore_pollset/perform_pollset, disconnect, write_resp, write_resp_hd, connection_is_dead, attach, and follow.

PROTOPT_* flags are the declarative knobs a new scheme uses to opt into behaviour — SSL, DUAL (two connections), NEEDSPWD, NOURLQUERY, WILDCARD, CREDSPERREQUEST, PROXY_AS_HTTP, CONN_REUSE, SSL_REUSE, NO_TRANSFER, HTTP_PROXY_TUNNEL — rather than special-casing the scheme in shared code.

New transport layers plug in as `struct Curl_cftype` instances; `Curl_cf_setup_add()` / `cf_setup_create()` build the base filter and the `cf_setup_add_*` helpers decide insertion order, so a new filter is added by writing one more `cf_setup_add_*` step.
Response-processing extensions register as `struct Curl_cwtype` with a `CURL_CW_*` phase; `cwriter_add()` inserts each writer first within its phase, so ordering is declared rather than coded.

Content and transfer decodings are two explicit registries — `general_unencoders[]` and `transfer_unencoders[]` — resolved by name in `find_unencode_writer()`, which is where a new `Content-Encoding` would be added alongside deflate/gzip/brotli/zstd/identity.

Upload-side extensions use the mirrored client-reader registry (`struct Curl_crtype` with `CURL_CR_*` phases); HTTP's Expect: 100-continue handling is implemented this way via `http_exp100_add_reader()`.

A new TLS backend is a `struct Curl_ssl` added to `available_backends[]` behind a `USE_*` define; `curl_global_sslset()` and the `CURL_SSL_BACKEND` lookup both iterate that same array, so no other file needs to change to make it selectable.

Resolver strategies are swappable at build time behind a common `lib/vdns/asyn.h` interface with three implementations — c-ares (`asyn-ares.c`), threaded (`asyn-thrdd.c`) and the shared base (`asyn-base.c`) — plus `cf-dns.c` exposing resolution as a connection filter.
SSH has two interchangeable backends selected at build time (libssh2 and libssh) behind lib/vssh/vssh.h, following the same one-directory-per-backend-family convention as vtls and vquic.

Adding a CLI option touches the alphabetically-sorted `aliases[]` table (the comment above it is explicit: "this array MUST be alphasorted based on the 'lname'"), the `C_*` id enum, a case in `getparameter()`, and the generated help in src/tool_listhelp.c.

New `--write-out` variables are one row in `variables[]` mapping a name to a `VAR_*` id, a `CURLINFO_*` id, and a writer function (`writeString`/`writeLong`/`writeOffset`/`writeTime`), with NULL signalling a special form handled inline.

New libcurl options plug into three parallel registries that must stay in sync: the `CURLOPT_*` enum in include/curl/curl.h, the typed setters in lib/setopt.c, and one curldown page under docs/libcurl/opts/ (422 of them) plus an entry in docs/libcurl/symbols-in-versions.

Multi-state entry hooks are themselves a small registry: the `state_enter[MSTATE_LAST]` function table in `mstate()` lets a state gain on-entry behaviour without touching `multi_runsingle()`'s switch.

Cross-handle caches are extended through the share interface: `share_setup()` in the tool shows the enumerable set (`CURL_LOCK_DATA_COOKIE`, `DNS`, `SSL_SESSION`, `PSL`, `HSTS`, `CONNECT`), and `CURLSHE_NOT_BUILT_IN` is tolerated so a disabled feature does not break setup.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat this repo as two coupled codebases with one very strict style contract. Read the internals docs before the code — docs/internals/ explains the four architectural ideas (connection filters, client writers, client readers, the multi state machine) that the code assumes you already know. Style is machine-enforced: `scripts/checksrc.pl` runs in CI and by default in debug builds, and a style violation fails the build before your logic is ever reviewed. Anything user-visible needs a matching curldown doc and usually a test case, and several files are generated and must not be hand-edited. The safest edits are additive table rows; the riskiest are changes to lib/multi.c, lib/url.c, lib/sendf.c, or lib/cfilters.c, which every protocol depends on.

claims.claim: Read first, in this order: docs/internals/README.md and the four core internals docs (CONNECTION-FILTERS.md, CLIENT-WRITERS.md, CLIENT-READERS.md, MID.md), then src/tool_main.c and src/tool_operate.c for the tool, then lib/easy.c and lib/multi.c for the library.

Style is non-negotiable and automated: docs/internals/CODE_STYLE.md is enforced by `scripts/checksrc.pl`, invoked via `make checksrc`, run automatically after `./configure --enable-debug`, and gated in CI by `scripts/checksrc-all.pl`.
`make lint` is the full pre-push check: it runs `scripts/badwords-all`, `make checksrc` across lib/src/tests/include/examples/projects, and `scripts/spacecheck.pl`.
Do not hand-edit generated files: src/tool_hugehelp.c is produced by src/mkhelp.pl from the manpage during the build, and src/tool_listhelp.c is likewise generated option-help data.

Docs are written in curldown (a markdown dialect with a YAML-ish front matter carrying `Title`, `Section`, `Added-in`, `See-also`), documented in docs/CURLDOWN.md and converted by scripts/managen; the checkdocs workflow validates them.
Adding a test means creating tests/data/testNNNN in the XML-like format and adding it to the numerically-ordered `TESTCASES` list in tests/data/Makefile.am — the file is not picked up automatically.

To run tests: `make test` (quiet) from the top, or drive the harness directly with `TFLAGS` — `cd tests && ./runtests.pl 1 to 200`, keyword selection like `FTPS` or `!feat:proxy`, `-t` for torture, and `make pytest` for the HTTP/2-3 python suite.

Public ABI is a hard boundary: include/curl/curlver.h carries the version macros, docs/libcurl/ABI.md states the compatibility promise, and docs/libcurl/symbols-in-versions records when every symbol appeared — new symbols must be added there.

Any new code must still compile with features disabled: wrap protocol/feature-specific code in the relevant `CURL_DISABLE_*` guard as documented in docs/CURL-DISABLE.md, and use `scripts/randdisable` to sanity-check random combinations.

Both build systems must be updated together: file lists live in lib/Makefile.inc and src/Makefile.inc for autotools and in lib/CMakeLists.txt / src/CMakeLists.txt for CMake, and configure-vs-cmake.yml exists to catch divergence.

Do not hand-write RELEASE-NOTES entries: it is maintained by scripts/release-notes.pl and the release flow in docs/RELEASE-PROCEDURE.md (the most recent commit on this branch is literally "RELEASE-NOTES: synced").
Never file a suspected vulnerability as a normal PR or issue: SECURITY.md and docs/VULN-DISCLOSURE-POLICY.md require private reporting through the curl disclosure process.

Trap: the `aliases[]` table in src/tool_getparam.c must stay alphabetically sorted by long name — `findlongopt()` binary-searches it, so an out-of-order insertion silently breaks option lookup rather than failing to compile.

Trap: tool code should call the `curlx_*` wrappers (`curlx_open`, `curlx_fopen`, `curlx_stat`, `curlx_strdup`, `curlx_safefree`, `curlx_dyn_*`) rather than libc directly — the wrappers carry the Windows/VMS/unicode portability that plain libc calls lose.

Trap: much of the interesting test machinery only exists in debug builds (`DEBUGBUILD`) — `curl_easy_perform_ev()`, `parallel_event()`, `CURL_FORBID_REUSE`, `CURL_MEMDEBUG`, `--test-duphandle` — so a change verified only against a release build has not been exercised by the full suite.

Safe edit boundaries: adding a row to a registry (schemes, filters, writers, aliases, writeout variables) is low-risk and local; edits inside lib/multi.c's state machine, lib/url.c's connection-reuse matching, or lib/sendf.c's writer stack affect every protocol at once and need the full suite plus pytest.
