readmePreview: HTTPie CLI: human-friendly HTTP client for the API era HTTPie (pronounced aitch-tee-tee-pie) is a command-line HTTP client.

overview.summary: HTTPie CLI is a Python-implemented, human-friendly command-line HTTP client that ships three console entry points -- `http`, `https`, and the `httpie` management interface -- all wired through `httpie.core.raw_main` (setup.cfg:70-74, httpie/core.py:32). Its distinguishing trait is a request-item mini-language (`Name:Value`, `name==value`, `field=value`, `field:=json`, `field@file`) that argparse parses into headers/params/data/files before delegating the actual transport to `requests` with HTTPie-specific adapters layered on top (httpie/cli/constants.py:15-27, httpie/client.py:43). Around that core sit a colorized/prettified output pipeline built on Pygments and Rich, JSON-file-backed sessions and config, a pip-driven plugin installer, and a detached background updater daemon. It targets API developers and shell scripters on Python 3.7-3.12 across Linux, macOS, and Windows, and is packaged for PyPI, Homebrew, Snap, Chocolatey, Fedora, and as a standalone PyInstaller binary.

system_map.summary: Three console_scripts entry points converge on a single error-handling shell: `http`/`https` map to `httpie.__main__:main` and `httpie` maps to `httpie.manager.__main__:main`, both of which call `httpie.core.raw_main` with a different parser and main_program. The package splits into `cli/` (argparse spec, request-item parsing, nested-JSON), `client.py` (requests glue), `output/` (streams, formatters, Rich UI), `sessions.py`/`config.py` (JSON persistence under the config dir), `plugins/` (entry-point registry), `manager/` (the `httpie` admin subcommands), and `internal/` (background update daemon). There is no database -- all state is JSON files under `$HTTPIE_CONFIG_DIR` or the XDG config dir. External integrations are the `requests`/`urllib3` stack, Pygments, Rich, defusedxml, requests-toolbelt, and `pip` shelled out for plugin installation. Build/test is Makefile-driven (`make install`, `make test`, `make codestyle`) with GitHub Actions running a 3-OS x 6-Python x pyopenssl matrix.

claims.claim: setup.cfg declares three console_scripts: `http` and `https` both point at `httpie.__main__:main`, while `httpie` points at `httpie.manager.__main__:main` -- the `https` alias is what makes `_process_url` default to the https:// scheme.

`httpie/__main__.py:main()` is a thin wrapper that imports `httpie.core.main` lazily, catches KeyboardInterrupt into `ExitStatus.ERROR_CTRL_C`, and returns `exit_status.value` -- keeping import cost off the Ctrl-C path.

`raw_main()` is the shared shell for both binaries: it sets `env.program_name`, decodes bytes argv via `decode_raw_args`, short-circuits into `run_daemon_task` when `--daemon` is present, loads installed plugins from `env.config.plugins_dir`, and prepends `config.default_options` to argv.

The CLI surface is declared declaratively as a `ParserSpec` of named `Group`s in httpie/cli/definition.py (Positional arguments, Predefined content types, Content processing options, Output processing, Output options, Sessions, Authentication, Network, SSL, Troubleshooting) and only then converted to argparse by `to_argparse()`.

`httpie/client.py:collect_messages()` is the transport boundary: it builds a `requests.Session` via `build_requests_session`, mounts `HTTPieHTTPAdapter` on http:// and `HTTPieHTTPSAdapter` on https://, plus any `TransportPlugin` prefixes, then yields PreparedRequest/Response pairs as a generator so output can stream.

Storage is JSON-file based via `BaseConfigDict`, which subclasses `dict`, writes with `json.dumps(indent=4, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=True)` and creates the parent dir with mode 0o700; `Config` (config.json) and `Session` (sessions/<host>/<name>.json) both derive from it.

Config-dir resolution is a four-step fallback: `$HTTPIE_CONFIG_DIR`, then `%APPDATA%/httpie` on Windows, then a legacy `~/.httpie` if it exists, then `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/httpie` (default `~/.config/httpie`).

The `httpie` manager binary owns a nested COMMANDS dict producing `httpie cli export-args`, `httpie cli check-updates`, `httpie cli sessions upgrade|upgrade-all`, and `httpie plugins install|upgrade|uninstall|list`; `generate_subparsers()` recursively materializes them into argparse subparsers.

`Environment` is the injected runtime boundary for all I/O -- stdin/stdout/stderr, isatty flags, encodings, color depth (probed via `curses.tigetnum('colors')`), Windows colorama stream wrapping, and lazily constructed Rich consoles -- which is precisely what the test suite overrides with `MockEnvironment`.

Build and test commands live in the Makefile: `make install` creates a venv and pip-installs `.[dev] .[test]` editable, `make test` runs pytest, `make test-cover` adds `--cov=httpie --cov=tests`, `make codestyle` runs flake8 over httpie/ tests/ extras/profiling/ docs/packaging/brew/, and `make build` swaps `__build_channel__.py` to `BUILD_CHANNEL = "pip"` before building the wheel.

pytest configuration is split across two files: setup.cfg sets `testpaths = httpie tests` with `--doctest-modules` (so module docstrings such as `ensure_path_as_is` and `humanize_bytes` are executable tests), while pytest.ini registers the `requires_installation` and `requires_external_processes` markers.

Deployment is many-target and workflow_dispatch-driven: release-pypi.yml publishes via `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish`, release-linux-standalone.yml runs `extras/packaging/linux/get_release_artifacts.sh` to produce a PyInstaller `http` binary plus .deb/.rpm, and .packit.yaml proposes the Fedora rawhide downstream update on release.

Generated content (man pages under extras/man/*.1 and the installation docs) is regenerated by `make content` and auto-PR'd by the content.yml workflow, using `extras/scripts/generate_man_pages.py` and `docs/installation/generate.py`.

`httpie/compat.py` is the portability boundary: it pins `is_windows`/`is_frozen`, back-fills `cached_property` for Python <3.8, switches between `importlib.metadata` and the `importlib_metadata` backport, and globally patches `cookiejar.DefaultCookiePolicy` to HTTPie's own policy.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing surface is one request-sending command with roughly fifty flags grouped into ten sections, plus a separate management binary with two command trees. Request construction supports JSON (default), form, multipart, raw body, nested-JSON keys, file embedding, and stdin piping. Output is controlled by a five-letter `--print` alphabet (H/B/h/b/m) with prettification, syntax highlighting, and streaming variants. Persistence features are named and anonymous sessions bound per host. Operational features include resumable downloads with Rich progress bars, offline request rendering, SSL/cipher/client-cert control, proxying, and a background update checker. Extensibility features are the four plugin categories plus a pip-backed plugin installer.

claims.claim: Request-item syntax is the headline feature: `:` headers, `;` empty header, `:@` header-from-file, `==` query params, `==@` query-from-file, `=` data string, `:=` raw JSON, `@` file upload, `=@` embed file contents, `:=@` embed raw JSON file -- each mapped to a dedicated processor function in `RequestItems.from_args`.

Nested-JSON keys (`foo[bar][0]=baz`) are a self-contained, dependency-free sub-language with its own tokenizer, recursive-descent `parse()` returning `Path` objects, and `interpret_nested_json()` builder; syntax errors surface as `NestedJSONSyntaxError` handled specially in `raw_main`.

Content-type modes are mutually exclusive via a `RequestType` enum: `--json/-j`, `--form/-f`, `--multipart` (with `--boundary`), and `--raw` for a literal body; `_process_request_type` expands the enum into the `args.json`/`args.form`/`args.multipart` booleans the rest of the code reads.

Output selection uses a compact alphabet -- `H` request headers, `B` request body, `h` response headers, `b` response body, `m` response metadata -- exposed via `--print`, with `--verbose` (=HBhb), `-vv` (all, incl. meta), `--headers`, `--body`, `--meta`, `--all`, and `--history-print` as shortcuts.

`--meta`/`-vv` prints an `Elapsed time` line computed as `response.elapsed` plus `monotonic() - response._httpie_headers_parsed_at`, i.e. header time plus body-read time, and is highlighted by a dedicated `MetadataLexer`.

Sessions come in two flavours: named sessions stored at `<config>/sessions/<host_port>/<name>.json`, and anonymous sessions triggered when the `--session` value contains a path separator, stored at the user-supplied path; `--session-read-only` loads without persisting back.

Download mode (`--download/-d`) implies `--follow`, moves normal output to stderr, derives a filename from Content-Disposition or the URL path (with mimetypes extension guessing and uniquifying `-N` suffixes), and supports `--continue` via a `Range: bytes=N-` header validated against the Content-Range response.

Download progress is rendered through Rich with three interchangeable displays -- `ProgressDisplay` when Content-Length is known, `StatusDisplay` (spinner) when it isn't, and `DummyDisplay` when `env.show_displays` is false (as in tests).

`--offline` renders the request without sending it: `collect_messages` yields the prepared request and never enters the send branch, and the parser flips default output options to `OUTPUT_OPTIONS_DEFAULT_OFFLINE` (request head + body).

Authentication ships three builtin plugins -- `basic` (unicode-safe latin1 header re-encoding), `digest`, and `bearer` (which sets `auth_parse = False` so the raw `-a` value becomes the token) -- and `--auth-type` choices are populated from the plugin registry.

SSL control includes `--verify` (yes/no/CA-bundle path), `--ssl` mapped through `AVAILABLE_SSL_VERSION_ARG_MAPPING` (ssl2.3 through tls1.3, filtered by what the local `ssl` module exposes), `--ciphers`, and client certs via `--cert`/`--cert-key`/`--cert-key-pass`.

`httpie plugins install/upgrade/uninstall/list` drives `pip install --prefer-binary --prefix=<plugins_dir> --no-warn-script-location` and implements uninstall by hand (unlinking `distribution.files`) because pip cannot uninstall from a custom prefix.

`httpie cli export-args --format json` serializes the whole ParserSpec (groups, aliases, choices, types, nested options) to JSON through `to_data()` -- the machine-readable contract used to generate docs and completions.

`--manual` prefers the system man page (`man 1 http`) when available and otherwise renders the Rich-formatted help through a pager; man-page availability can be disabled with the `HTTPIE_NO_MAN_PAGES` env var.

Prettification is a plugin chain of four builtin `FormatterPlugin`s -- HeadersFormatter (stable sort), JSONFormatter (re-indent/sort via `load_prefixed_json`), XMLFormatter (defusedxml-backed pretty printing), and ColorFormatter (Pygments) -- toggled by `--pretty` and tuned by `--format-options`.

data_flow.summary: Input arrives from four boundaries -- argv, stdin, files referenced by request items, and the JSON config/session files -- and is normalized inside `HTTPieArgumentParser.parse_args`, which mutates a single `argparse.Namespace` through an ordered chain of `_process_*` methods. `RequestItems.from_args` fans the raw `KeyValueArg` list into four typed multi-dicts (headers, data, params, files) plus a multipart ordering dict. `client.collect_messages` then translates the namespace into `requests.Request` kwargs, applies session headers/cookies/auth, prepares the request, optionally deflates it, and yields message objects lazily. Output flows back through `OutputOptions.from_message` into `write_message`, which picks a stream class (Raw/Encoded/Pretty/BufferedPretty) and writes bytes to `env.stdout.buffer`. On the way out, session cookies and headers are re-materialized and written back to JSON.

claims.claim: The parse pipeline is strictly ordered and order-dependent: `_apply_no_options` -> `_process_request_type` -> `_process_download_options` -> `_setup_standard_streams` -> `_process_output_options` -> `_process_pretty_options` -> `_process_format_options` -> `_guess_method` -> `_parse_items` -> `_process_url` -> `_process_auth` -> `_process_ssl_cert`, followed by stdin/`--raw` body ingestion.

`config.default_options` is prepended to argv (not merged post-parse), so user defaults behave exactly like typed flags and can be individually reverted with the generic `--no-OPTION` mechanism implemented in `_apply_no_options`.

Method inference is data-driven: with no METHOD, POST is chosen if there is stdin/`--raw` input else GET; when the first positional is not alphabetic, the parser re-interprets it as a request item and shifts URL/method, then chooses POST if any item separator is in `SEPARATOR_GROUP_DATA_ITEMS`.

In JSON mode, nested-JSON items are split out first via `split_iterable` and interpreted as a batch (so `[]` append semantics work across items), while all remaining items are processed one-by-one into their target dicts.

Headers use `HTTPHeadersDict`, a case-insensitive multidict where `add(key, None)` means 'explicitly unset'; `finalize_headers` later converts `None` values for urllib3's SKIPPABLE_HEADERS into `SKIP_HEADER` and strips/encodes all other values.

Because `requests`' PreparedRequest collapses duplicate headers, `apply_missing_repeated_headers` re-injects the original repeated values after preparation, skipping any field that was overridden along the way.

Default headers are computed from the request shape: User-Agent is always `HTTPie/<version>`, JSON mode adds `Accept: application/json, */*;q=0.5` and `Content-Type: application/json`, and form mode without files adds `application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=utf-8`.
Session headers are merged beneath CLI headers (`headers.update(base_headers)` then `headers.update(args.headers)`), so a header typed on the command line always wins over the stored session value.

Request bodies are normalized by `prepare_request_body`: str/bytes become bytes, `RequestDataDict` becomes urlencoded bytes, file-likes go through `_prepare_file_for_upload`, and `--chunked` wraps everything in a `ChunkedUploadStream`/`ChunkedMultipartUploadStream` generator.

Upload progress is echoed back to stdout through a callback loop: `program()` passes `request_body_read_callback` into `collect_messages`, which threads it into `prepare_request_body`, which wraps `file.read` so each chunk is re-emitted via `write_raw_data`.

Redirects are handled manually rather than by requests: `allow_redirects` is hard-set to False in `make_send_kwargs`, and `collect_messages` walks `response.next` itself so that each hop can be yielded for `--all`/`--history-print` and counted against `--max-redirects`.

Response bytes are decoded adaptively: `EncodedStream` uses the declared charset if present, otherwise accumulates `charset_normalizer` guesses and locks one in after `ENCODING_GUESS_THRESHOLD` (3) consecutive agreeing guesses; bodies containing NUL bytes raise `BinarySuppressedError` and print the 'binary data not shown' notice instead.

Session write-back materializes runtime state into serializable JSON: `post_process_data` converts the `RequestsCookieJar` into a list of dicts keeping only name/expires/path/value/domain/secure, and the header multidict into a list of `{name, value}` objects, each passed through the corresponding legacy exporter.

Expired cookies are pruned on the way out: every response's `Set-Cookie` is scanned by `get_expired_cookies`, which translates `max-age` into `expires` (a workaround for a requests bug) and returns name/path pairs that `Session.remove_cookies` deletes before saving.

Headers written to a session deliberately drop request-specific fields: anything prefixed `Content-` or `If-`, the HTTPie-generated User-Agent, and `Cookie` (whose morsels are diverted into the cookie jar instead).

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows carry most of the behaviour. Startup walks __main__ -> core.raw_main -> plugin loading -> parser.parse_args -> check_updates -> core.program. The primary request flow walks program -> collect_messages -> requests.Session.send -> OutputOptions.from_message -> write_message -> stream class -> stdout buffer, message by message, as a generator so headers can print before the body arrives. Persistence walks get_httpie_session -> Session.load -> pre_process_data (with legacy fixups) -> update_headers -> save -> post_process_data. A fourth notable flow is the update daemon, which double-forks out of the main process to fetch a version index without blocking the user.

claims.claim: Startup, step by step: `__main__.main()` imports `core.main`, which imports `httpie.cli.definition.parser` and calls `raw_main(parser, program, argv, Environment())`; `raw_main` sets `env.program_name`, calls `decode_raw_args`, checks `is_daemon_mode`, calls `plugin_manager.load_installed_plugins`, prepends default options, then `parser.parse_args(args, env)`.

`--debug` is handled before parsing: `print_debug_info` writes HTTPie/Requests/Pygments/Python/platform versions plus `repr(env)` and `repr(plugin_manager)` to stderr, and a bare `http --debug` returns SUCCESS without ever building a request.

After a successful parse, `check_updates(env)` runs before `main_program`; the `_update_checker` decorator wraps it so that every exception is swallowed by `suppress(BaseException)` unless `developer_mode` is set in config.json.

Primary request trace: `program()` builds `ProcessingOptions.from_raw_args`, optionally constructs a `Downloader` and calls `downloader.pre_request(args.headers)`, then iterates `collect_messages(env, args, request_body_read_callback)`, calling `OutputOptions.from_message` and `write_message` per message.

Inside `collect_messages` the order is: resolve session -> `make_request_kwargs` -> `make_send_kwargs` -> `build_requests_session` -> apply session headers/cookies/auth -> `requests.Request(**kwargs)` -> `session.prepare_request` -> `transform_headers` -> `ensure_path_as_is` (if `--path-as-is`) -> `compress_request` (if `--compress`) -> yield/send loop.

`max_headers` is a context manager that temporarily monkey-patches `http.client._MAXHEADERS` around the single `session.send()` call so `--max-headers` can exceed the stdlib's default cap, restoring it in a finally block.

Write trace: `write_message` -> `build_output_stream_for_message` -> `get_stream_type_and_kwargs` picks RawStream (non-tty, no prettify), EncodedStream (tty, no prettify), PrettyStream (`--stream` or `text/event-stream` auto-detect) or BufferedPrettyStream, then `write_stream` pushes each chunk to `outfile.buffer`, flushing when tty or streaming.

`BaseStream.__iter__` defines the on-wire ordering for one message: headers, then `\r\n\r\n`, then body chunks (each fed to `on_body_chunk_downloaded`), then -- if `--meta` -- a blank line and the metadata block.

Message separation is stateful: `program()` tracks `prev_with_body` and `force_separator`, emitting `MESSAGE_SEPARATOR_BYTES` between messages when the previous one had a body and either output is redirected or a streamed upload forced it.

Download trace: after the response loop, `downloader.start(initial_url, final_response)` builds a `RawStream` over the response with `chunk_downloaded` as the progress callback, `write_stream` drains it to the output file, `downloader.finish()` stops the display, and a size mismatch sets `downloader.interrupted` and an error exit status.

Session persistence trace: `get_httpie_session` resolves the bound hostname (falling back to `localhost` for hostname-less URLs), builds the path, and calls `Session.load()`, which runs `read_raw_config` then `pre_process_data` -- importing cookies into a `RequestsCookieJar` with `HTTPieCookiePolicy` and headers into an `HTTPHeadersDict`.

On the way out, the session is saved only when it is new or `--session-read-only` was not used: cookies are replaced with the requests session jar, expired cookies removed, then `save()` writes JSON and stamps `__meta__.httpie` with the current version.

Update-daemon trace: `maybe_fetch_updates` checks the 2-week FETCH_INTERVAL, calls `spawn_daemon('fetch_updates')`, which on POSIX double-forks, calls `setsid()`, closes stdio, and re-enters `httpie.core.main(['http', 'fetch_updates', '--daemon'])` -- except on Darwin, where it spawns a subprocess instead because double-fork is unreliable there.

Manager trace with a confusing invocation: `manager.__main__.main` calls `raw_main(use_default_options=False)`; if argparse raises, `is_http_command()` silently re-parses the args with the http parser inside `env.as_silent()` and, on success, prints the 'use http/https instead' hint before returning ERROR.

Session upgrade trace: `httpie cli sessions upgrade <host> <name>` loads the session with warnings suppressed, selects fixers whose version is greater than the stored `__meta__.httpie` (3.1.0 cookie-format, 3.2.0 header-format), applies them in order, and calls `save(bump_version=True)`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is pytest-based with pytest-httpbin providing a real local HTTP/HTTPS server, plus `responses`, `pytest-mock` and a hand-rolled `http_server` fixture for cases httpbin cannot express. Roughly 6,600 lines across ~35 test modules under tests/, exercising the CLI end-to-end through a `MockEnvironment` that swaps stdin/stdout for temp files and disables colors and progress displays. `--doctest-modules` means docstring examples inside httpie/ are also collected. Coverage is strongest on sessions, output, JSON, uploads, and CLI parsing; weakest on the daemon-spawning internals, Rich help/palette rendering, and the manager plugin installer (which is gated behind a `requires_installation` marker). CI runs the suite across 3 OSes x 6 Python versions x pyopenssl on/off, with a separate coverage job and a flake8 style job.

claims.claim: The suite runs real HTTP against pytest-httpbin: conftest.py auto-uses an `httpbin_add_ca_bundle` fixture that monkeypatches `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` to pytest-httpbin's cert, and adds an `httpbin_secure_untrusted` variant that deliberately removes it for negative TLS tests.

`tests/utils/__init__.py` defines the `MockEnvironment` harness: colors=0, stdout/stdin as temp files, `show_displays=False`, plus an `Encoder`/`FakeBytesIOBuffer` pair that smuggles undecodable binary output through a text stream as `hash(N)` placeholders.
Tests globally disable the updater by setting `Config.DEFAULTS['disable_update_warnings'] = True` at import time, explicitly to stop hundreds of subprocesses hitting the network during a run.

Two pytest markers gate the expensive tests: `requires_installation` (all of tests/test_plugins_cli.py and tests/test_httpie_cli.py, which shell out to a real install) and `requires_external_processes` (parts of test_uploads.py and test_update_warnings.py), with pytest.ini documenting how to deselect them.

tests/utils/http_server.py provides a decorator-registry `TestHandler` over `BaseHTTPRequestHandler` with `handlers[method][path]`, used for behaviours httpbin cannot produce -- notably cookie-on-redirect semantics.

The largest test modules by line count are test_sessions.py (852), test_output.py (631), test_json.py (583), test_uploads.py (403), test_cli.py (377) and test_httpie.py (372) -- i.e. persistence, rendering, and the request-item language get the most attention.

Plugin extension points are covered by executable examples rather than mocks: test_transport_plugin.py registers a `FakeTransportPlugin` with prefix `http+fake`, asserts the fake adapter's response renders correctly, and unregisters it in a finally block.

The ParserSpec serialization contract has a golden-output test asserting the exact JSON shape (options, is_optional, is_variadic, metavar, choices, python_type_name), which is what protects `httpie cli export-args` consumers.

A dedicated `tests/utils/matching` package (parsing.py, tokens.py, test_matching.py) exists to assert on tokenized terminal output, letting colorized output be checked structurally instead of by brittle ANSI string comparison.

`--doctest-modules` in setup.cfg means library docstrings are part of the suite -- e.g. `ensure_path_as_is`, `humanize_bytes`, `KeyValueArgType.tokenize`, and `detect_encoding` all carry assertions that fail the build if behaviour drifts.

tests.yml runs the full matrix of {ubuntu-latest, macos-13, windows-latest} x Python {3.7..3.12} x pyopenssl {0,1}, with `fail-fast: false`; Windows runs pytest directly while Linux/macOS go through `make install && make test`.

The pyopenssl matrix dimension is wired through `HTTPIE_TEST_WITH_PYOPENSSL`, which a session-scoped autouse fixture reads to call `urllib3.contrib.pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3()` and hard-fails if the module is missing.
Coverage runs only on pull_request via coverage.yml (`make test-cover` then `make codecov-upload` with CODECOV_REPO_TOKEN, followed by `make test-dist` to verify sdist and wheel installs).
Style is enforced separately by code-style.yml running `make codestyle` -> flake8 with only E501 and W503 ignored, over httpie/, tests/, extras/profiling/ and docs/packaging/brew/.

Performance regressions have an opt-in path rather than a gate: benchmark.yml only runs when a PR is labeled `benchmark`, executing `extras/profiling/run.py --fresh --complex --min-speed=6` and posting the pyperf results as a PR comment.

risk_map.summary: The sharpest edges are in code that leaves the process or touches the filesystem outside the repo: the update daemon double-forks and re-executes the CLI, the plugin installer shells out to pip and then unlinks files by hand, and man-page display execs `man`. TLS handling has two deliberate-but-loud decisions -- a global `urllib3.disable_warnings()` and a `verify=False` fetch of the version index. Filesystem risk concentrates in download filename derivation and lock-file handling in the system temp dir. Structurally, `core.program()` and `_process_auth()` are both flagged in-repo as needing refactoring, and the argparse Namespace is a mutable god-object threaded through most modules, so changes to parse ordering have wide blast radius.

claims.claim: `_fetch_updates` performs `requests.get(PACKAGE_INDEX_LINK, verify=False)` against https://packages.httpie.io/latest.json -- an unauthenticated, certificate-unverified network call whose result drives the version-comparison warning shown to users.

`client.py` calls `urllib3.disable_warnings()` unconditionally at import, which silences InsecureRequestWarning process-wide -- including for `--verify=no` -- so a user disabling verification gets no library-level warning.

Daemon mode is decided by a raw substring check (`'--daemon' in args`) before argparse ever runs, so the flag is reachable from ordinary argv; the blast radius is limited only by the `assert options.task_id in DAEMONIZED_TASKS` in `run_daemon_task`, and asserts vanish under `python -O`.

`_spawn_posix` double-forks, calls `os.setsid()`, closes stdin/stdout/stderr, and then re-enters `httpie.core.main(['http'] + args)` in-process with `suppress(BaseException)` -- a path that is effectively untestable in-process and whose failures are silent by construction.

`spawn_daemon` copies the full parent environment into the child process context and injects a computed `PYTHONPATH` derived from `inspect.stack()[0][1]`, so anything in the caller's env (including secrets) is inherited by the detached process.

`PluginInstaller._uninstall` deletes files directly with `os.unlink(distribution.locate_file(file))` for every entry in `distribution.files`; the only guard is a check that `self.dir` is in `base_dir.parents`, and the code's own TODO notes failures are not rolled back.

`_clear_metadata` calls `shutil.rmtree(meta_path)` on `.dist-info`/`.egg-info` directories whose version differs from the freshly installed one, driven by parsing the last line of pip's stdout (`Successfully installed ...`) -- a string-parsing dependency on pip's output format.

Plugin loading executes arbitrary third-party code at startup: `load_installed_plugins` calls `entry_point.load()` for every matching entry point, catching only `BaseException` into a warning -- so a malicious or broken plugin on the plugins path runs on every `http` invocation.

Download filenames are attacker-influenced: `filename_from_content_disposition` takes the server-supplied header and sanitizes it only with `os.path.basename(...).lstrip('.').strip()`, after which `get_unique_filename` opens the result for append in the current working directory.

`open_with_lockfile` derives a lock path as base64 of the target path inside the shared system temp dir and relies on `touch(exist_ok=False)` for mutual exclusion; the lock is only removed in the finally block, so a hard kill leaves a stale lock that permanently raises `LockFileError` for that file.

Credentials flow into session files: when `--auth` is given alongside `--session`, `collect_messages` writes `{'type': auth_type, 'raw_auth': plugin.raw_auth}` into the session JSON, meaning plaintext `user:password` is persisted to disk under the config directory.

`_process_auth` also silently harvests credentials from two implicit sources -- a `user:pass@host` URL and the user's netrc via `get_netrc_auth` (for plugins with `netrc_parse = True`, i.e. basic and digest) -- unless `--ignore-netrc` forces an `ExplicitNullAuth`.

Two subprocess shell-outs exist outside the plugin installer: `man_pages.is_available`/`display_for` run `man 1 <program_name>` with `env.program_name` derived from argv[0], and the linux packaging build invokes `pyinstaller` via `subprocess.check_call`.

Two central functions carry explicit in-repo refactor warnings: `core.program()` is marked 'TODO: Refactor and drastically simplify, especially so that the separator logic is elsewhere' and `_process_auth` is marked 'TODO: refactor & simplify this method' -- both are on every request path.

`_setup_standard_streams` mutates `env.stdout`/`env.stdout_isatty` in place during parsing (redirecting stdout to stderr for `--download`, to devnull for `--quiet`), so any later code that captured the original stream sees stale state -- a fragile coupling the code itself labels 'FIXME: Come up with a cleaner solution'.

The legacy session-format modules are live compatibility shims rather than dead code -- `pre_process`/`post_process` run on every session load and save, and the 3.1.0 fixer exists because domainless cookies were a documented security problem.

`HTTPieCookiePolicy` widens cookie security by treating `localhost` and `*.localhost` as secure origins, so `Secure` cookies are sent over plain http to those hosts -- intentional (mirrors Firefox) but a deviation from the stdlib default that affects every request.

extension_points.summary: Extension is designed around four setuptools entry-point groups consumed by a single `PluginManager`, which is itself just a `list` subclass with typed filters. Built-in behaviour is registered through the same mechanism, so formatters and auth methods are not special-cased. Beyond plugins, the CLI itself is data: `ParserSpec`/`Group`/`Argument` describe the interface declaratively, the manager's COMMANDS dict describes subcommands, and `CLI_TASKS` and `DAEMONIZED_TASKS` are plain dict dispatch tables. Adding output behaviour means either a FormatterPlugin or a new `BaseStream` subclass selected in `get_stream_type_and_kwargs`.

claims.claim: The four plugin entry-point groups are `httpie.plugins.auth.v1`, `httpie.plugins.converter.v1`, `httpie.plugins.formatter.v1` and `httpie.plugins.transport.v1`, mapped to their base classes in `ENTRY_POINT_CLASSES`; adding a fifth category means editing that dict.

`plugin_manager` is a module-level singleton in httpie/plugins/registry.py where all builtins are registered (BasicAuthPlugin, DigestAuthPlugin, BearerAuthPlugin, HeadersFormatter, JSONFormatter, XMLFormatter, ColorFormatter) -- the canonical place to add a new builtin.

`PluginManager` exposes `register`/`unregister`/`filter` plus typed accessors (`get_auth_plugins`, `get_auth_plugin_mapping`, `get_formatters_grouped`, `get_converters`, `get_transport_plugins`), making runtime registration in tests a two-line operation.

A new `AuthPlugin` needs only `auth_type` plus `get_auth()`, and can tune behaviour through the class-level switches `auth_require`, `auth_parse`, `netrc_parse`, and `prompt_password` -- all of which `_process_auth` consults.
`TransportPlugin` extension is prefix-based: `build_requests_session` mounts `plugin.get_adapter()` at `plugin.prefix`, which is how httpie-unixsocket-style schemes (e.g. `http+unix://`) plug in.

`FormatterPlugin` subclasses declare a `group_name` ('format' by default, 'colors' for ColorFormatter) and are collected by `get_formatters_grouped`; `Formatting.__init__` then instantiates only the groups named by `--pretty` and keeps those whose `self.enabled` is true.

`ConverterPlugin` is the hook for binary payloads: `Conversion.get_converter(mime)` asks each registered converter's `supports(mime)` classmethod, and PrettyStream/BufferedPrettyStream call it when they hit a NUL byte, turning what would be a 'binary suppressed' notice into rendered text.

New CLI flags are added declaratively to a `Group` in httpie/cli/definition.py (with `short_help`, `help`, and optional `nested_options`), never by touching argparse directly -- `to_argparse` strips the HTTPie-only keys listed in `ARGPARSE_IGNORE_KEYS` before delegating.

Dynamically computed choice lists use the custom `lazy_choices` argparse action registered in `to_argparse`, so expensive enumerations (available Pygments styles, auth types, SSL versions) are only materialized when help or export-args is requested.

New manager subcommands plug into two places: the nested `COMMANDS` dict in httpie/manager/cli.py (which `generate_subparsers` walks recursively) and the `CLI_TASKS` dispatch dict in httpie/manager/tasks/__init__.py keyed by action name.

Background work plugs into `DAEMONIZED_TASKS`, a name->callable dict in daemon_runner.py; `_check_status` is an example entry that exists purely so tests can assert the spawn path works without touching the network.
New session-format migrations plug into `FIXERS_TO_VERSIONS`, a version-string -> `fix_layout` callable mapping consulted by `upgrade_session` via `is_version_greater`.

New request-item separators plug into the `rules` dict inside `RequestItems.from_args`, which maps each separator constant to a (processor_func, target_dict) tuple -- plus membership in the relevant frozenset in cli/constants.py.

New output stream behaviour plugs into `get_stream_type_and_kwargs`, the single factory that maps (isatty, prettify groups, stream flag, message type) onto RawStream / EncodedStream / PrettyStream / BufferedPrettyStream and their kwargs.

Colour themes plug in via `make_styles()`, which generates one header style and one body style per entry in `SHADE_TO_PIE_STYLE` and merges the resulting names into `BUNDLED_STYLES` that `--style` offers.

agent_handoff.summary: Read httpie/core.py, httpie/cli/argparser.py, httpie/client.py and httpie/cli/definition.py before touching anything -- those four hold the control flow, the mutation order, the transport glue, and the CLI contract. The project is conservative: contributions without tests are explicitly rejected, behaviour changes require documentation, and CHANGELOG.md is maintained by hand. Generated artefacts (extras/man/*.1, docs/installation/README.md) must never be hand-edited. The safest edit boundaries are adding a new plugin, adding a declarative flag to a group in definition.py, or adding a formatter; the riskiest are reordering `_process_*` calls, changing the `collect_messages` generator contract, and anything in httpie/internal/.

claims.claim: Read first, in this order: httpie/core.py (both entry shells), httpie/cli/argparser.py (the ordered mutation chain), httpie/client.py (requests translation), httpie/cli/definition.py (the flag contract), and httpie/context.py (the I/O boundary every test overrides).

CONTRIBUTING.md is explicit that PRs with code changes but no tests will generally not be merged, and that behaviour changes need documentation -- treat a failing or absent test as a blocker, not a nice-to-have.

Local workflow is `make install` (creates ./venv and pip-installs the dev+test extras editable), then `make test`; for a single module use the venv's pytest directly, and `make codestyle` before pushing since a separate CI job enforces flake8.

Never hand-edit extras/man/*.1 or docs/installation/README.md -- both are generated by `make content` (via extras/scripts/generate_man_pages.py and docs/installation/generate.py) and auto-PR'd by the content.yml workflow.

Man-page generation sets `HTTPIE_BUILDING_MAN_PAGES=1` before importing httpie, which flips `IS_MAN_PAGE` in definition.py so machine-specific defaults (e.g. the computed `--ciphers` list) are excluded -- any new environment-dependent default must respect that flag.

Add CLI flags only through `group.add_argument(...)` in httpie/cli/definition.py using `Qualifiers.*` instead of raw argparse constants; `to_argparse` translates them and `serialize()` exports them, so a raw argparse string will break `httpie cli export-args`.

Every `--OPTION` automatically gets a `--no-OPTION` counterpart handled by `_apply_no_options`, which resets `args.<dest>` to the action's default -- so new flags must have a meaningful `default`, not rely on absence.

Trap: the order of `_process_*` calls in `parse_args` is load-bearing. `_setup_standard_streams` must run before `_process_output_options` (which reads `env.stdout_isatty`), and `_parse_items` must run before `_process_url`/`_process_auth`. Reordering silently changes defaults.

Trap: `collect_messages` is a generator whose laziness is the streaming contract -- the session save at the end only runs if the caller exhausts it, so wrapping it in anything that short-circuits will silently stop sessions from persisting.

Trap: do not print with `print()` or touch `sys.stdout` directly. All output must go through `env.stdout`/`env.stderr` or the Rich consoles, because `--quiet`, `--output`, `--download` and the whole test harness swap those streams.

Trap: `--doctest-modules` is on, so any docstring in httpie/ containing a `>>>` prompt is a test. Editing `humanize_bytes`, `ensure_path_as_is`, `detect_encoding` or `KeyValueArgType.tokenize` means updating their examples too.

Trap: tests hit the network by design. `pie.dev` is used for chunked-upload and remote tests via the `httpbin_with_chunked_support` and `remote_httpbin` fixtures, which skip (not fail) when DNS does not resolve -- a green local run may simply have skipped them.

Safe edit boundary: adding a formatter, converter, auth or transport plugin touches only httpie/plugins/registry.py plus the new module, and existing plugin tests show the register/unregister pattern.

Risky edit boundary: httpie/internal/ (daemons.py, daemon_runner.py, update_warnings.py) forks processes and swallows every exception via `_get_suppress_context`; set `developer_mode: true` in config.json to surface errors while working there.

Version and release conventions: `httpie/__init__.py` holds `__version__` (3.2.4) and `__date__`, setup.cfg reads it via `attr:`, the Makefile refuses to publish a version containing 'dev', and `make build` rewrites `internal/__build_channel__.py` to `BUILD_CHANNEL = "pip"` for the PyPI artifact.
Security-relevant changes have a disclosure path rather than a public issue: SECURITY.md directs reports to security@httpie.io or huntr.dev with a reproducer, severity and CWE id.

overview.summary: jsonwebtoken is Auth0's reference Node implementation of RFC 7519 JSON Web Tokens, published to npm as `jsonwebtoken` v9.0.3. It is a tiny, dependency-light library (three public functions — `sign`, `verify`, `decode` — plus three error classes) that wraps `jws` for the actual JWS signing/verification and layers on claim semantics (exp/nbf/aud/iss/sub/jti/nonce/maxAge), option schema validation, and a hard-won set of key-confusion defenses. What is distinctive is how much of the code is defensive rather than functional: roughly half of sign.js and verify.js is dedicated to coercing untrusted key material into `crypto.KeyObject`s, rejecting alg/key-type mismatches (the classic RS256→HS256 confusion attack), and enforcing a 2048-bit RSA modulus floor. It targets any Node service that issues or consumes JWTs, and ships both callback-async and synchronous-throwing modes of every entrypoint.

system_map.summary: This is a pure library with no server, no database, and no network I/O of its own — the only runtime boundary is the Node `crypto` module and the `jws` package. `index.js` is the whole public API surface: it re-exports `decode.js`, `verify.js`, `sign.js`, and the three error classes from `lib/`. Support modules in `lib/` are all single-purpose: feature-detection booleans gated on `process.version` via `semver`, a `ms`-backed timespan parser, and the asymmetric key/algorithm compatibility matrix. Build is nonexistent (plain CommonJS, no transpile); test is `mocha`, coverage is `nyc mocha --use_strict`, lint is `eslint .`. Deployment is npm publish driven by `semantic-release` in a two-workflow release dance on `master`.

claims.claim: `index.js` is the sole entrypoint and exports exactly six symbols: `decode`, `verify`, `sign`, `JsonWebTokenError`, `NotBeforeError`, `TokenExpiredError` — there is no class, no factory, no configuration object.

All cryptography is delegated to the `jws` package (`^4.0.1`): `jws.decode` in decode.js, `jws.sign`/`jws.createSign` in sign.js, and `jws.verify` in verify.js. This repo contains no hashing, HMAC, or signature code of its own.

The runtime dependency set is deliberately minimal and old-school: `jws`, `ms`, `semver`, and seven separately-published single-function lodash packages (`lodash.includes`, `lodash.isboolean`, `lodash.isinteger`, `lodash.isnumber`, `lodash.isplainobject`, `lodash.isstring`, `lodash.once`).

Node version capability is resolved at require-time, not call-time, by three boolean modules that `semver.satisfies(process.version, ...)`: `lib/psSupported.js` (`^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0`), `lib/asymmetricKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=15.7.0`), and `lib/rsaPssKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=16.9.0`).

PS256/PS384/PS512 are spliced into the algorithm allow-lists at module load only when `PS_SUPPORTED` — into `SUPPORTED_ALGS` at index 3 in sign.js, and appended to both `PUB_KEY_ALGS` and `RSA_KEY_ALGS` in verify.js.

The error hierarchy is hand-rolled ES5 prototype inheritance, not `class extends Error`: `JsonWebTokenError` calls `Error.call(this, message)` and manually sets `this.message`, and `NotBeforeError`/`TokenExpiredError` do `Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and add a `date`/`expiredAt` field.

`lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` owns the key-type↔algorithm compatibility matrix (`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` for `ec`/`rsa`/`rsa-pss`) and the ES-curve mapping (`allowedCurves`: ES256→prime256v1, ES384→secp384r1, ES512→secp521r1). It is the single shared gate called by both sign and verify.

`lib/timespan.js` is the only time-arithmetic module; it converts a `ms`-parseable string or a raw number into an absolute epoch-seconds timestamp, and returns `undefined` (not an error) for unparseable input, pushing error construction onto its three callers.

Developer commands are `npm test` (bare `mocha`), `npm run coverage` (`nyc mocha --use_strict`), `npm run lint` (`eslint .`), and `npm run update-changelog` (`conventional-changelog -p conventionalcommits -i CHANGELOG.md`). `npm run prepare` installs husky hooks.

CI is five GitHub Actions workflows: `test.yml` (PR-triggered matrix over Node 16/18/20/22/24), `commitlint.yml` (PR-triggered conventional-commit validation), `prepare-release.yml` and `release.yml` (both on push to master, mutually exclusive via a `chore(release):` head-commit-message guard), and `sca-scan.yml` (Snyk, via a pinned reusable workflow from `auth0/devsecops-tooling`).

Publishing is `semantic-release` configured in `.releaserc.json` on the `master` branch, with conventional-commits analysis, npm publish from repo root, a `prepareCmd` of `git diff --exit-code`, and a `verifyReleaseCmd` that runs a ReversingLabs `rl-wrapper` scan over the `npm pack` tarball before release.

The published npm tarball is narrowed by the `files` allow-list to `lib`, `decode.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js` — tests, `bin/`, and workflows never ship. `.npmignore` additionally excludes `opslevel.yml`.

Repo ownership/routing is declared for Auth0 internal tooling: `CODEOWNERS` assigns everything to `@auth0/project-iam-protocols-engineer-codeowner` and `opslevel.yml` tags the repo to the `iam_protocols` owner.
`package.json` declares `engines.node >= 12`, but the test matrix only exercises Node 16 through 24 — the 12/14 support claim is unverified by CI.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing surface is three functions, each with a dual sync/async calling convention selected by whether a trailing callback is supplied. `sign` turns a payload plus key into a compact JWS, mapping option names onto registered claim names and computing time-based claims. `verify` is the security-critical path: it re-decodes, resolves a key (possibly via an async key-lookup callback for JWKS/kid workflows), enforces an algorithm allow-list, checks key/alg compatibility, verifies the signature, then runs seven independent claim checks. `decode` is the deliberately unauthenticated escape hatch. Twelve signing algorithms plus `none` are supported, and a set of explicit backwards-compatibility escape valves (`allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`) let callers opt out of the newer hardening.

claims.claim: `jwt.sign(payload, secretOrPrivateKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options validated by `sign_options_schema`: `expiresIn`, `notBefore`, `audience`, `algorithm`, `header`, `encoding`, `issuer`, `subject`, `jwtid`, `noTimestamp`, `keyid`, `mutatePayload`, `allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` — and rejects any key not in that schema with `"<key>" is not allowed in "options"`.

Four sign options are sugar that write registered claims, via the `options_to_payload` table: `audience`→`aud`, `issuer`→`iss`, `subject`→`sub`, `jwtid`→`jti`. Supplying both the option and the raw claim is an error (`Bad "options.<x>" option. The payload already has an "<claim>" property.`).

Non-object payloads (strings, numbers, Buffers) are supported for signing but reject the seven object-only options listed in `options_for_objects` with `invalid <opts> option for <typeof> payload`; a Buffer payload round-trips as its string form.
`mutatePayload: false` (the default) shallow-clones the payload with `Object.assign({}, payload)` before adding `iat`/`exp`/`nbf`, which is what makes signing a frozen or sealed payload work.
`options.encoding` (default `utf8`) is passed through to `jws`, so `{encoding: 'binary'}` produces a differently-encoded payload segment for non-ASCII characters.

`jwt.verify(token, secretOrPublicKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options: `algorithms`, `audience`, `complete`, `issuer`, `jwtid`, `ignoreExpiration`, `ignoreNotBefore`, `subject`, `clockTolerance`, `maxAge`, `clockTimestamp`, `nonce`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`.

`secretOrPublicKey` may be a key-lookup function `(header, cb)` — the JWKS/`kid` integration point — but only when a callback is also supplied; otherwise verify fails with `verify must be called asynchronous if secret or public key is provided as a callback`.
Audience matching accepts a string, a `RegExp`, or an array of either, and matches if ANY token `aud` entry matches ANY expected audience — an any-to-any `some`/`some` cross product.

`clockTolerance` (seconds of slack) and `clockTimestamp` (override for "now") apply to `nbf`, `exp`, and `maxAge` uniformly; `clockTimestamp` must be a number or verify fails early with `clockTimestamp must be a number`.

`maxAge` is an independent expiry ceiling computed from `payload.iat`, requires a numeric `iat` (`iat required when maxAge is specified`), and cannot loosen `exp` — a token past `exp` still fails even with `maxAge: '1000y'`.
`complete: true` on either `verify` or `decode` returns `{header, payload, signature}` instead of the bare payload — this is how callers reach `kid` and `alg` for key selection.
`jwt.decode(token, options)` performs no signature verification at all, and silently swallows a `JSON.parse` failure on the payload — returning the raw string payload rather than throwing.

Unsigned (`alg: none`) tokens are supported on both sides but require explicit opt-in on verify: `please specify "none" in "algorithms" to verify unsigned tokens`, and passing a key alongside a signature-less token yields `jwt signature is required`.

Two named backwards-compatibility escape hatches exist and are documented as discouraged: `allowInsecureKeySizes` (permits RSA modulus < 2048) and `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` (skips the `validateAsymmetricKey` gate).

data_flow.summary: There are exactly two input boundaries — the caller-supplied `(payload | jwtString, key, options)` tuple — and one output boundary, either a returned/thrown value or a `(err, result)` callback invocation. No state is owned across calls: the library is entirely stateless, with the only module-level mutable structures being the algorithm allow-list arrays built at require time. The central transform on both paths is key normalization: whatever the caller passes (string, Buffer, PEM, JWK-ish object) is funnelled through `crypto.createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey` with a `createSecretKey` fallback into a `KeyObject`, and every downstream decision reads `key.type`, `key.asymmetricKeyType`, and `key.asymmetricKeyDetails` off that normalized object. Claim data flows one way on sign (options → payload properties → JWS) and one way on verify (JWS → decoded payload → claim assertions → returned payload).

claims.claim: On sign, key material normalization is a try/catch cascade: if not already a `KeyObject`, attempt `createPrivateKey(secretOrPrivateKey)`, fall back to `createSecretKey(Buffer.from(...))` for strings, and on double failure emit `secretOrPrivateKey is not valid key material`.

Verify mirrors that cascade with `createPublicKey` then `createSecretKey`, producing `secretOrPublicKey is not valid key material` — this is what converts a hostile object with a throwing `toString` into a clean error instead of arbitrary execution.

The JWS header is assembled by `Object.assign` with a fixed precedence: computed `{alg, typ, kid}` first (alg defaults to `HS256`, `typ` is `'JWT'` only for object payloads, `kid` comes from `options.keyid`), then `options.header` spread last so it can override any of them including `alg`.

A single `timestamp` value — `payload.iat || Math.floor(Date.now()/1000)` — is computed once and is the base for both `nbf` and `exp`, guaranteeing the three time claims are internally consistent within one sign call.

On verify, the token is parsed twice: once shallowly as `jwtString.split('.')` for arity (`jwt malformed` when length !== 3) and signature-presence checks on `parts[2]`, and once fully through `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})`.

`options` is defensively shallow-cloned on entry to verify (`Object.assign({}, options)`) specifically because the function later writes `options.algorithms` when the caller omitted it — caller-supplied objects are never mutated.

When `options.algorithms` is absent, the allow-list is derived from the normalized key: `secret`→HS_ALGS, `rsa`/`rsa-pss`→RSA_KEY_ALGS, `ec`→EC_KEY_ALGS, everything else→PUB_KEY_ALGS. This binds the accepted alg set to the key material, not to the token.

The token-supplied `header.alg` flows into `jws.verify(jwtString, decodedToken.header.alg, secretOrPublicKey)`, but only after passing the allow-list membership check and the key-type compatibility check — the ordering at lines 144→152→165 is the whole defense.

The verified `payload` object returned to the caller is the same object produced by `decode`, not a copy — all seven claim checks read from it without transforming it, so callers receive attacker-influenced data verbatim (the README explicitly warns to sanitize it).

Both functions funnel every error through a single sink — `failure(err)` in sign and `done(err, data)` in verify — which dispatches to `callback(err)` when async or `throw err` when sync, so sync and async modes are guaranteed to produce identical errors.

`decode` normalizes the payload channel: `jws.decode` may return a string payload, which `decode` opportunistically `JSON.parse`s and keeps only if the result is a non-null object — otherwise the string passes through unchanged.

`timespan(time, iat)` is the shared conversion from relative to absolute time on both paths: it feeds `payload.nbf`/`payload.exp` on sign and `maxAgeTimestamp` on verify, using `ms()` for strings and plain addition for numbers.
The only file-system reads in the entire repo are in tests, loading PEM fixtures from `test/*.pem` — the library itself performs zero file or network I/O.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows matter: module load (feature detection), signing, and verification. Module load is unusual in that it bakes Node-version capability into module-scope constants, so the same code path behaves differently on Node 14 vs Node 16 without any runtime branch. Signing is a long linear gauntlet of eleven guards before any crypto happens. Verification is the inverse-ordered gauntlet, and its ordering is load-bearing: algorithm allow-listing and key-type checks must both precede `jws.verify`. Both entry functions branch at the very end into callback vs synchronous return.

claims.claim: MODULE LOAD: `require('jsonwebtoken')` → index.js requires decode/verify/sign → sign.js requires `lib/psSupported` → `semver.satisfies(process.version, '^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0')` → if true, `SUPPORTED_ALGS.splice(3, 0, 'PS256','PS384','PS512')` executes at module scope. Algorithm support is therefore frozen at first require.

SIGN step 1-2: normalize arity (`typeof options === 'function'` → shift to callback), compute `isObjectPayload` as `typeof payload === 'object' && !Buffer.isBuffer(payload)`, then build `header` via `Object.assign`.
SIGN step 3-4: reject missing key unless `algorithm === 'none'`, then coerce to `KeyObject` via `createPrivateKey` → `createSecretKey` fallback.

SIGN step 5: enforce symmetry — `header.alg.startsWith('HS')` requires `key.type === 'secret'`; `/^(?:RS|PS|ES)/` requires `key.type === 'private'`; and for non-ES RSA algs, `asymmetricKeyDetails.modulusLength < 2048` is rejected (guarded by an `!== undefined` check for pre-Node-15 where the field is absent).

SIGN step 6-8: `validatePayload` (allowUnknown=true, checks only iat/exp/nbf are numbers) → clone payload unless `mutatePayload` → reject `exp`+`expiresIn` and `nbf`+`notBefore` double-specification → `validateOptions` (allowUnknown=false).

SIGN step 9-11: `validateAsymmetricKey(header.alg, key)` unless opted out → compute `timestamp` and apply `noTimestamp`/`iat` → `timespan` for `nbf` and `exp` → copy the four `options_to_payload` claims.

SIGN terminal branch (async): wrap callback in `once()`, then `jws.createSign({header, privateKey, payload, encoding})` with `.once('error', callback)` and `.once('done', ...)`; the done handler re-checks `signature.length < 256` as a pre-Node-15 proxy for the 2048-bit modulus rule.

SIGN terminal branch (sync): `jws.sign({header, payload, secret, encoding})` returns the token, followed by the identical `signature.length < 256` check which `throw`s rather than calling back. Both branches carry a `TODO: Remove ... once node 15+ is the minimum supported version`.

VERIFY step 1-4: arity normalization → clone options → build `done` (callback or throw-on-error closure) → validate `clockTimestamp`/`nonce`/`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` shapes → compute `clockTimestamp` → reject falsy or non-string `jwtString` → split into exactly 3 parts.

VERIFY step 5-6: `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})` inside a try/catch (returns `invalid token` if falsy), then choose `getSecret` — either the caller's key-lookup function or a trivial wrapper that immediately yields the static key. All remaining logic runs inside that callback.

VERIFY step 7: the three-way signature/key presence matrix — signature-without-key → `secret or public key must be provided`; key-without-signature → `jwt signature is required`; neither-plus-no-algorithms → `please specify "none" in "algorithms"`.

VERIFY step 8-10 (the security core, in this exact order): coerce key → derive default `algorithms` from key type → reject `header.alg` not in the list (`invalid algorithm`) → reject HS-alg-with-non-secret-key and RS/PS/ES-alg-with-non-public-key → `validateAsymmetricKey` → only then `jws.verify`.

VERIFY step 11 (claims, in order): `nbf` (type check then `> clockTimestamp + clockTolerance` → `NotBeforeError`) → `exp` (→ `TokenExpiredError`) → `audience` → `issuer` → `subject` → `jwtid` → `nonce` → `maxAge` (→ `TokenExpiredError('maxAge exceeded')`) → return payload or the `complete` triple.

KEY-CONFUSION TRACE: an attacker-forged `{alg: HS256, kid: rsaKeyId}` token presented with the legitimate RSA public key reaches line 148, where `header.alg.startsWith('HS') && key.type !== 'secret'` throws `secretOrPublicKey must be a symmetric key when using HS256` — before `jws.verify` is ever called. The test asserts this for both KeyObject and PEM forms.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is the strongest part of the repo: ~258 `it()` blocks across 30 mocha files in `test/`, backed by chai assertions, sinon fake timers, and 17 checked-in PEM fixtures covering RSA, RSA-PSS, EC (three curves), DSA, and deliberately-invalid keys. The signature move is `test/test-utils.js`, which runs every sign/verify twice — once sync, once async — under a frozen clock and asserts the two produce byte-identical tokens or deep-equal errors; this is why the sync/async parity invariant actually holds. Coverage is configured with hard nyc thresholds, but the CI workflow runs bare `mocha`, so those thresholds and eslint are never enforced on PRs. Test naming is split between a per-claim convention (`claim-*.test.js`, `option-*.test.js`) and older topic/regression files (`*.tests.js`, `issue_*.tests.js`).

claims.claim: The framework stack is mocha 5 + chai 4 + sinon 6, with `atob` used to independently decode base64url segments in encoding tests. There is no `.mocharc`, so mocha's default `./test/*.js` glob picks up every file in `test/`.

`test/test-utils.js` exports `signJWTHelper` and `verifyJWTHelper`, both of which freeze time with `sinon.useFakeTimers({now: Date.now()})`, run the sync call in a try/catch, then run the async call and assert equality of token or error before restoring the clock.

`expectEqualError` exists because chai does not deep-equal errors (the helper cites chaijs/chai#1009); it compares `message` and `name` explicitly plus every enumerable property, which is how `expiredAt`/`date` payloads on the error subclasses get verified.

Option/claim validation is tested exhaustively by table-driven loops over ~15 bad values (`true, false, null, -1.1, Infinity, NaN, ' ', '', [], ['foo'], {}, {foo:'bar'}` …), applied per-claim in `claim-exp.test.js`, `header-kid.test.js`, and siblings.
`test/claim-aud.test.js` is the largest test file at 436 lines and 36 `it()` blocks, reflecting that audience matching (string/regex/array cross-product) is the most branch-heavy claim check.

`test/jwt.asymmetric_signing.tests.js` is parameterized: it builds an `algorithms` map of RS256/ES256 (plus PS256 when `PS_SUPPORTED`) each with `pub_key`, `priv_key`, and an `invalid_pub_key` that is deliberately not the pair of `priv_key`, then runs the same describe block per algorithm.
Security regressions are explicitly locked in by `test/jwt.malicious.tests.js`: HMAC-with-RSA-key confusion (both KeyObject and PEM form) and the malicious-`toString` Buffer-impersonation RCE vector.

Historical bugs are pinned by dedicated regression files: `issue_70.tests.js` (PEM headers), `issue_147.tests.js` (signing an `Object.seal`ed payload), `issue_304.tests.js`, and `rsa-public-key.tests.js`.

`test/validateAsymmetricKey.tests.js` unit-tests the key-matrix module directly (not through sign/verify), including the no-key and no-algorithm short-circuit paths and the PS/curve branches gated on the feature-detection booleans.
nyc is configured with `check-coverage: true` and thresholds of 95% lines, 95% statements, 100% functions, 95% branches, excluding `./test/**` — a genuinely strict bar.

GAP: `test.yml` runs only `npm test` (bare mocha). Neither `npm run coverage` nor `npm run lint` appears in any workflow, so the nyc thresholds and the eslint ruleset are advisory only and can silently regress.

A known-broken case is parked rather than fixed: `it.skip('should work with none algorithm where secret is falsy')` in async_sign, annotated with a link to node-jws issue #62 — the async `alg: none` path with a falsy secret is untested and known not to work.

A coverage hole is deliberately carved out with `/* istanbul ignore next */` around the entire `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` block in validateAsymmetricKey, with a comment explaining it would otherwise sink coverage on Node < 15.7.0 — meaning EC curve matching and RSA-PSS parameter checks are excluded from the coverage numbers.

Test fixtures include intentionally-bad keys used as negative cases: `invalid_pub.pem`, `ecdsa-public-invalid.pem`, `rsa-pss-invalid-salt-length-private.pem`, and `dsa-public.pem` (to assert `Unknown key type "dsa".`).

risk_map.summary: As a library whose entire job is security, nearly every line in verify.js is a security-sensitive path, and the ordering of its checks is the load-bearing invariant — any reordering that lets `jws.verify` run before the algorithm allow-list check reintroduces the classic JWT confusion attacks. The most concrete correctness defect is in sign.js's `options_to_payload` loop, where `return failure(...)` inside a `forEach` callback does not abort the enclosing function, so in async mode the callback can fire twice. Secondary risks cluster around Node-version-conditional code that CI does not fully exercise, deliberately silent error swallowing in `decode`, a very old eslint pinned at v4, and release workflows that handle several third-party secrets. Blast radius for any change here is unusually wide: this package sits in the dependency tree of a large fraction of Node auth stacks.

claims.claim: CORRECTNESS BUG: in the `options_to_payload` loop, `return failure(...)` only returns from the `forEach` arrow — the outer sign function continues. In async mode `failure` invokes the raw callback with an error at line 221, and since `callback` is not yet wrapped by `once()` (that happens at line 230), signing proceeds and the callback is invoked a second time with a valid token.

SECURITY-CRITICAL ORDERING: the allow-list check (`options.algorithms.indexOf(header.alg) === -1`), the key-type symmetry check, and `validateAsymmetricKey` all sit between `decode` and `jws.verify`. Any edit that moves `jws.verify` earlier, or that trusts `header.alg` before line 144, reopens the RS256→HS256 confusion class.

`options.header` is `Object.assign`ed LAST when building the sign header, so a caller passing `{header: {alg: 'none'}}` silently overrides `options.algorithm` — and the downstream key/alg checks then run against the overridden value. This is by design but is a sharp edge for callers who build headers from user input.

`decode` swallows all `JSON.parse` errors in an empty `catch (e) { }`, returning the raw string payload instead. Callers that assume an object back from `decode` will see a string on malformed tokens with no signal.

The `signature.length < 256` heuristic is an acknowledged stopgap for the 2048-bit modulus rule on Node < 15, duplicated in both the sync and async branches with matching `TODO: Remove ...` comments — a two-site invariant that can drift.

No source file uses `'use strict'`, so sloppy-mode semantics apply — e.g. `delete payload.iat` on a primitive string payload under `noTimestamp` is a silent no-op rather than a TypeError. Notably `npm run coverage` runs mocha with `--use_strict` while `npm test` does not, so the two commands exercise different semantics.

The EC curve check dereferences `key.asymmetricKeyDetails.namedCurve` without a null guard; it is protected only by the module-load `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` semver boolean, and that whole block is excluded from coverage by `istanbul ignore next`.

The verified payload returned by `verify` is the same object `decode` produced, unsanitized and fully attacker-controlled in content; the README carries an explicit warning to treat it as user input, which implies downstream misuse is a known recurring problem.

`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes: true` disables `validateAsymmetricKey` on both sign and verify, and a test asserts it lets an ES256-labelled token be processed with an RSA key — a documented footgun kept only for backwards compatibility.

`release.yml` handles six secrets (`PRODSEC_TOOLS_ARN`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_USER`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_TOKEN`, `RLSECURE_LICENSE`, `RLSECURE_SITE_KEY`, `SIGNAL_HANDLER_TOKEN`) and embeds credentials in a pip `--index-url`. Mitigations are in place — `persist-credentials: false`, `mask-aws-account-id: true`, SHA-pinned actions — but this job is the highest-value supply-chain target in the repo.

`prepare-release.yml` parses the next version out of semantic-release's human-readable stdout with `awk '/The next release version is/{print $NF}'` — a brittle coupling to log wording that would silently produce an empty version if the message text changes.

DEAD CODE: `bin/changelog` is a standalone conventional-changelog script with hardcoded `releaseCount: 19` and a commented-out `preset: 'jshint'`, but nothing references it — `package.json` and `prepare-release.yml` both go through the `update-changelog` npm script instead (per commit b924272).

STALE TOOLING: `eslint` is pinned at `^4.19.1` (with `ecmaVersion: 6` in the parser options, below the ES2018+ syntax the sources actually use), and `nsp@^2.6.2` — a long-deprecated security tool — remains a devDependency with no script invoking it.

The README still advertises Travis CI and david-dm badges even though CI has moved to GitHub Actions, and the TODO section admits `X.509 certificate chain is not checked` — a real, documented limitation for anyone using x509 PEMs as verification keys.

The `files` allow-list omits `index.js` despite it being `main`; npm force-includes the `main` file so the package works today, but the list is one refactor (e.g. moving the entry to `lib/`) away from shipping a broken tarball.

extension_points.summary: This library has no plugin system by design — a JWT implementation with third-party extension hooks would be a security liability. What it does have are a handful of declarative tables that are the intended edit sites for new capability, and one genuine runtime hook. The tables are the two option schemas and the `options_to_payload` map in sign.js, the four algorithm arrays in verify.js, and the `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`/`allowedCurves` matrices in `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` — adding an algorithm means touching all three files coherently. The one caller-facing hook is verify's function-valued `secretOrPublicKey`, which is where JWKS clients plug in. Feature detection for new Node capabilities follows a one-file-per-boolean convention in `lib/`.

claims.claim: PRIMARY RUNTIME HOOK: `secretOrPublicKey` as a `(header, secretCallback)` function is the documented integration point for JWKS/`kid`-based key resolution; internally the static-key case is normalized into the same shape so there is exactly one code path after line 101.

Adding a new sign option means one entry in `sign_options_schema` with an `isValid` predicate and a `message` — the generic `validate(schema, allowUnknown, object, parameterName)` walker requires no other change, and unknown options are rejected because `validateOptions` passes `allowUnknown: false`.

`registered_claims_schema` is the parallel table for payload claims and is validated with `allowUnknown: true`, so arbitrary custom claims pass through while `iat`/`exp`/`nbf` are type-enforced — this asymmetry is the extension point for application-specific claims.

`options_to_payload` is a two-column map from option name to claim name; adding a new registered-claim shortcut is a one-line addition there, and the conflict-detection and copy logic applies automatically.

`options_for_objects` is the companion list declaring which options are meaningless for non-object payloads; any new object-only option must be added here too or it will be silently accepted on a string payload.

Algorithm support is defined in four arrays: `SUPPORTED_ALGS` (sign.js) and `PUB_KEY_ALGS` / `EC_KEY_ALGS` / `RSA_KEY_ALGS` / `HS_ALGS` (verify.js). A new algorithm requires edits in both files plus `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`.

`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` maps `asymmetricKeyType` → permitted `alg` values and is the single authority on key/algorithm pairing; an unrecognized key type throws `Unknown key type "<type>"`, so new key types must be registered here or they are rejected outright.
`allowedCurves` maps ES algorithms to required named curves and is the place to add a curve; it is consulted only under `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED`.

New Node-version feature gates follow a one-module-per-flag convention: a three-line file exporting `semver.satisfies(process.version, '<range>')`, consumed as a module-scope constant. Three such files already exist.

New error types extend the hierarchy by the ES5 pattern in `lib/NotBeforeError.js`: call `JsonWebTokenError.call(this, message)`, set `this.name`, add the payload field, then `prototype = Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and restore `constructor`. New types must also be re-exported from `index.js` to be reachable.

New verify-time claim checks slot into the linear block between `jws.verify` and the return, following the established `if (options.X) { if (payload.y !== options.X) return done(new JsonWebTokenError(...)) }` shape used by issuer/subject/jwtid/nonce.

Test convention for new options/claims: add a `test/option-<name>.test.js` or `test/claim-<name>.test.js` file that uses `testUtils.signJWTHelper`/`verifyJWTHelper` plus `asyncCheck`, so sync/async parity is enforced for free.

Release automation is itself extensible through `.releaserc.json`'s plugin array; the `@semantic-release/exec` entry is where additional pre-publish gates (currently `git diff --exit-code` and the ReversingLabs scan) would be added.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat this as a security library first and a JavaScript project second: the check ordering in verify.js and the guard cascade in sign.js are the product, and reordering them is never a safe refactor even when it looks like cleanup. Style is intentionally conservative CommonJS ES5/ES6 with no build step, no TypeScript, no async/await, and no strict mode — match it rather than modernize it. Read the four root JS files and `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` before touching anything; they are under 600 lines combined. Commits must be Conventional Commits because commitlint gates PRs via husky locally and a workflow in CI, and because semantic-release derives the version from them.

claims.claim: READ FIRST, in order: `index.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js`, `decode.js`, `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js`. That is the entire library — under 600 lines total — and everything else in `lib/` is a three-line helper.

RUN: `npm test` for the fast loop (mocha over `test/`), `npm run coverage` before proposing a merge (nyc enforces 95/95/100/95 and will fail the command), and `npm run lint` manually since no workflow runs it.

COMMIT FORMAT: Conventional Commits are mandatory. `.husky/commit-msg` runs `npx --no -- commitlint --edit $1` locally and `commitlint.yml` re-validates every commit in a PR range; `@commitlint/config-conventional` is the ruleset.

STYLE: 2-space indent enforced by both `.editorconfig` and the eslint `indent` rule; no semicolon rule, no quote rule. eslint is pinned at v4 with `ecmaVersion: 6`, so avoid syntax newer than ES2015 in new code paths or the lint run will fail to parse.

TRAP — check ordering: in verify.js, lines 144 (allow-list), 148-152 (key-type symmetry), and 154-160 (key/alg matrix) must all remain before line 165 (`jws.verify`). Moving or short-circuiting any of them is a vulnerability, not a refactor.

TRAP — dual calling convention: every change to sign or verify must work identically in sync (throws) and async (callback) mode. `test/test-utils.js` asserts byte-equality of tokens and deep-equality of errors across the two, so a one-sided fix will fail loudly.

TRAP — `return` inside `forEach`: the existing `options_to_payload` loop already has this bug (a `return failure(...)` that does not abort the function). Do not copy that pattern into new claim-copy logic, and be aware that fixing it changes observable async callback behavior.

TRAP — Node-conditional code: three `semver.satisfies` booleans are evaluated at module load. Code behind `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` and `RSA_PSS_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` will not execute on your local Node unless it is new enough, and is excluded from coverage — verify such changes against the CI matrix (16/18/20/22/24), not just locally.

SAFE EDIT BOUNDARY: adding a claim check, a validated option, or a test is low-risk and well-patterned. Changing key coercion (`createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey`/`createSecretKey` cascades), the algorithm arrays, or `validateAsymmetricKey` is high-risk and touches published security behavior.

DO NOT EDIT casually: `CHANGELOG.md` is generated by `npm run update-changelog` during the prepare-release workflow, and `package.json` `version` is bumped by `npm version --no-git-tag-version` in that same workflow. Hand-editing either will conflict with the release automation.

RELEASE SHAPE: pushing to master triggers `prepare-release.yml`, which opens a `release/vX.Y.Z` PR titled `chore(release): X.Y.Z`; merging that PR matches the `startsWith(..., 'chore(release):')` guard and triggers `release.yml` to run `npx semantic-release`. The two workflows are mutually exclusive by that guard.

New public API or option changes must be reflected in `README.md`, which is the only user documentation and is structured as `jwt.sign` / `jwt.verify` / `jwt.decode` / Errors & Codes / Algorithms supported.
Any PR touching `lib/`, `sign.js`, or `verify.js` will require review from `@auth0/project-iam-protocols-engineer-codeowner` — the CODEOWNERS glob is `*`, so every path is covered.

Do not add PEM fixtures casually: 17 already exist covering RSA, RSA-PSS (valid and invalid salt length), EC on three curves, DSA, and invalid public keys — reuse them via the `loadKey(filename)` helper convention.

Security vulnerabilities must not be filed as GitHub issues — the README directs them to Auth0's Responsible Disclosure Program. An agent discovering one should report it to the user rather than opening a public issue.
